title: What chemistry studies
description: Chemistry is the study of matter: what it is made of (composition), how it looks and behaves (properties) and how it changes when it meets other matter (interactions).

facts.text: Chemistry is the study of the composition, properties and interactions of matter: what things are made of and how they change.
A substance's properties include how it looks and behaves, such as its hardness and whether it burns (flammability).

title: Chemistry began in kitchens and workshops
description: People practiced chemistry long before it was a science: controlling fire to cook, fire pottery and smelt metals, and fermenting food and drink.

facts.text: Humans began to practice chemistry when they learned to control fire and use it to cook, make pottery and smelt metals; cooking, fermentation, glass making and metalworking date from the beginnings of civilization.

title: Chemistry, the central science
description: Chemistry is called the central science because it connects to so many other fields, from biology (through biochemistry) to medicine, materials and the environment.

facts.text: Chemistry is sometimes called "the central science" because it connects with many other fields, such as biology, medicine, materials science, forensics and environmental science.
Chemistry and biology meet in biochemistry, the study of the substances in living things and how they change.
Digesting food, making the polymers used in clothing and credit cards, and refining crude oil into gasoline are all examples of chemistry.

title: What counts as matter
description: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space: an ant, a truck, a galaxy, and invisible air too.

facts.text: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space (occupies volume), from an ant to a truck to a whole galaxy.
Gases are matter too: if gases did not take up space, a balloon would not get bigger when filled with gas.
Dry air has a density of about 1.2 grams per liter, so the 50,000 liters of air in a room 4 m by 5 m with a 2.5 m ceiling has a mass of about 60 kilograms.

title: Mass is not weight
description: Mass is the amount of matter in something; weight is the pull of gravity on it. On the Moon an astronaut weighs one-sixth as much but has the same mass.

facts.text: Mass is the amount of matter in an object; weight is the pull of gravity on it. On the Moon, whose gravity is one-sixth of Earth's, an astronaut has the same mass but one-sixth the weight.

title: Solid, liquid and gas
description: A solid is rigid with a definite shape and volume; a liquid flows and takes its container's shape but keeps its volume; a gas takes both the shape and volume of its container.

facts.text: A solid is rigid with a definite shape and volume; a liquid flows and takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume; a gas takes both the shape and the volume of its container.

title: Particles explain the states
description: Matter is made of tiny particles. In a solid they are packed tight and vibrate in place; in a liquid they are close but slide past each other; in a gas they are far apart and move freely.

facts.text: All matter is made of tiny particles: atoms, which can join into molecules.

In a solid, particles are tightly packed, often in a regular pattern, and vibrate about fixed positions; in a liquid they stay close but move past each other; in a gas they are far apart and move independently except when they collide.

title: What melting and boiling do to particles
description: Heating gives particles more energy. Enough energy frees them from fixed places (melting) or from their neighbors entirely (boiling). While a substance changes state, its temperature holds steady.

facts.text: Heating raises the kinetic energy of particles, so they move faster; with enough energy they overcome the attractions holding them, and the substance melts or boils.
While a substance is changing state, such as ice melting or water boiling, its temperature stays constant: the heat goes into pulling particles apart rather than speeding them up.
Ice, liquid water and steam are the same substance, water, in different states.

title: Boiling points depend on pressure
description: Water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at sea-level pressure. Boiling happens when the vapor pushes back as hard as the air pressing down, so with less air pressure (up a mountain) water boils cooler, about 90 °C in Leadville, Colorado.

facts.text: Ice melts at 0 °C, and water boils at 100 °C at sea-level air pressure (1 atmosphere).
A liquid boils when its vapor pushes out as hard as the surrounding pressure pushes in, so lower air pressure means a lower boiling point.
In Leadville, Colorado, about 10,200 feet (3,100 m) up in the Rocky Mountains, water boils at about 90 °C, about 10 °C below its sea-level boiling point.
Melting points shift with pressure too, but far less: water's melting point drops only slightly as pressure rises.

title: Plasma, the fourth state
description: Plasma is a gas so energized that electrons are torn from its atoms, leaving a mix of electrically charged particles that conducts electricity. Heat or high voltage, like lightning, makes it.

facts.text: Plasma, a fourth state of matter, is a gas containing many electrically charged particles; it forms when electrons (tiny charged particles from inside atoms) are torn free from gas atoms, for example by intense heat, and it conducts electricity.
Lightning turns the air in its path into plasma; high-voltage electricity can tear electrons free.
Lightning can heat the air in its channel to about 50,000 °F, about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

title: Plasma fills the universe
description: The Sun and other stars are mostly plasma, so nearly all the visible matter in the universe is plasma, even though on Earth we meet it mainly in lightning and auroras.

facts.text: Nearly all the visible matter in the universe is plasma, because the Sun and other stars are mostly plasma; this counts ordinary matter, not dark matter.
On Earth, natural plasma appears in lightning and in the aurora, the glowing curtains of light near the poles.

title: Mixtures and pure substances
description: A mixture is two or more kinds of matter mingled in amounts that can vary, and it can be separated by physical means. A heterogeneous mixture, like a chocolate chip cookie, is not the same all the way through.

facts.text: A mixture is two or more kinds of matter mingled in amounts that can vary, and it can be separated by physical means; a pure substance always has the same composition.
A heterogeneous mixture is not the same all the way through; chocolate chip cookies, granite and Italian salad dressing are examples.

title: Solutions
description: A solution is a homogeneous mixture, the same all the way through. The dissolved substance is the solute and the one doing the dissolving is the solvent. Solutions can be liquids, gases (air) or solids (brass).

facts.text: A homogeneous mixture, the same all the way through, is called a solution; salt water, maple syrup, gasoline and air are examples.
In a solution, the substance that gets dissolved is the solute and the one doing the dissolving is usually called the solvent; you can add more solute only up to a limit, its solubility.
Solutions need not be liquid: air is a solution of mostly nitrogen and oxygen, and brass is a solid solution of copper and zinc.

title: Filtering and evaporating
description: Mixtures are separated by physical differences. A filter holds back solid bits like sand but lets dissolved salt through with the water; evaporating the water then leaves the salt behind.

facts.text: Mixtures can be separated by physical methods such as filtration, evaporation and distillation, which use differences in the parts' physical properties.
Filtration removes solid particles from a liquid or gas using a filter that lets the fluid through but holds back the solids, as when brewing coffee.
In a sand, salt and water mixture, the sand stays behind as a solid while the dissolved salt goes along with the water, so filtering alone cannot remove the salt.
Evaporating the water from a salt solution leaves the salt behind; in many parts of the world, table salt is obtained by evaporating seawater.

title: Distillation
description: Distillation heats a liquid to vapor and cools the vapor back to liquid somewhere else. Because parts of a mixture turn to vapor at different temperatures, it can make fresh water from seawater.

facts.text: Distillation turns a liquid into vapor and then condenses the vapor back into liquid; because the parts of a mixture boil at different temperatures, the lowest-boiling part comes off first.
Distillation can produce fresh water from seawater, leaving the salt behind.
More than 2,300 years ago, Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) noted that evaporating seawater makes pure water.

title: Density
description: Density is mass divided by volume: how much mass is packed into each bit of space. Water is about 1 gram per cubic centimeter.

facts.text: Density is an object's mass divided by its volume: how much mass is packed into a given space, so equal masses can take up very different volumes.
Liquid water has a density of about 1 gram per cubic centimeter.

title: Float or sink
description: An object floats if its average density is less than the liquid's and sinks if it is denser. Weight alone does not decide it: a big log floats while a small iron nail sinks.

facts.text: An object floats if its average density is less than that of the liquid around it and sinks if it is denser.
Wood floats on water because it is less dense than water, while iron sinks because it is denser.
The fraction of a floating object that sits below the surface equals its density compared with the liquid's, so ice, only a little less dense than water, floats mostly submerged.

title: Why ice floats
description: Frozen water molecules lock into an open, spread-out pattern, so ice is only about 90 percent as dense as liquid water, and it floats. Salty seawater is denser still.

facts.text: Ice is less dense than liquid water, about 90 percent as dense (about 0.92 versus 1.0 grams per cubic centimeter), which is why ice floats.
When water freezes, its molecules lock into an open lattice that spreads them farther apart than in the liquid; water is unusual in this.
Dissolved salt makes seawater denser than pure water.

title: Physical change
description: In a physical change, matter changes form or state but stays the same substance: melting, boiling, tearing, grinding. Boiling water bubbles, but it is still water.

facts.text: In a physical change, matter changes its form or state but not its identity; melting wax or ice, boiling water, tearing paper and grinding a solid into powder are physical changes.
Clues to a chemical change include an unexpected color change, a new smell, heat or light given off, and gas bubbles; but boiling also makes bubbles without making any new substance.

title: Chemical change
description: In a chemical change at least one new substance forms: rusting, burning, cooking meat, a banana browning. Chemical changes are often harder to undo.

facts.text: In a chemical change at least one new substance forms; iron rusting, a match or candle burning, meat cooking and a banana browning are chemical changes.
When a candle burns, the wax reacts to form new substances, carbon dioxide and water.
Chemical changes are often harder to reverse than physical ones.

title: Gray areas between the two kinds of change
description: The line between physical and chemical change is not perfectly sharp. Dissolving salt is usually called physical, yet some chemists argue otherwise; and reversibility is no sure test, since a rechargeable battery reverses a chemical change.

facts.text: The distinction between physical and chemical change is not clear cut; some science educators describe it as more of a continuum, and salt dissolving in water is a debated case.
Salt dissolving in water is usually classified as a physical change, though the dissolved salt comes apart into charged particles in the water.
Reversibility is not a reliable test: a rechargeable battery reverses a chemical change each time it is charged.

title: Sublimation and deposition
description: Some solids turn straight into gas (sublimation): dry ice at normal pressure, and snow slowly even below freezing. The reverse, gas straight to solid, is deposition, as in frost. Both are physical changes.

facts.text: Sublimation is a solid turning straight into a gas; dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) sublimes at normal air pressure instead of melting, and snow and ice slowly sublime below freezing, faster in wind and the low pressure of high altitudes.
Deposition is the reverse of sublimation, a gas turning straight into a solid; frost forming is an example.

title: The ancient Greek idea of atoms
description: Leucippus and Democritus reasoned, without experiments, that cutting matter must stop at uncuttable particles, atoms. Aristotle disagreed, and a scientific atomic theory came only in the 1800s.

facts.text: In the 5th century BCE, Leucippus and his student Democritus proposed that all matter is made of tiny particles called atoms.
The word atom comes from the Greek for "indivisible" or "uncuttable".
The atomists argued that finishing an endless division would leave either still-divisible specks or nothing, so division must stop at atoms.
The Greek philosophers treated atoms as a philosophical idea and apparently never tested it with experiments.
Aristotle rejected atoms: he held that matter could be divided forever and was made of fire, earth, air and water.
A scientific atomic theory explaining how matter behaves, John Dalton's, arrived only in the early 1800s; it was first published in 1807.
Leucippus and Democritus proposed atoms about 2,400 years ago, in the 5th century BCE.

title: Atoms and the void
description: Democritus pictured atoms moving through empty space, differing only in shape, arrangement, position and size, like letters that build every word.

facts.text: Democritus held that the world is atoms moving in empty space (the void), differing only in shape, arrangement, position and size.
Ancient accounts compared atoms to letters: A differs from N in shape, and AN differs from NA in arrangement.
Democritus said sweet, bitter, hot and cold exist only "by convention"; in reality there are only atoms and void.

title: Protons, neutrons and electrons
description: Atoms are built from positive protons and neutral neutrons in the nucleus, with negative electrons around it. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, and the proton count identifies the element.

facts.text: Atoms are built from protons (positive) and neutrons (no charge) in a central nucleus, with electrons (negative) around it.
A neutral atom has the same number of electrons as protons, so its charges balance.
The number of protons in the nucleus (the atomic number) defines the element: any atom with 6 protons is carbon.

title: The nucleus holds the mass
description: Protons and neutrons have almost the same mass and are far heavier than electrons, so nearly all of an atom's mass is in its nucleus.

facts.text: It takes about 1,800 electrons to equal the mass of one proton.
Protons and neutrons have almost the same mass.
Nearly all of an atom's mass is in its nucleus, because protons and neutrons are much heavier than electrons.

title: How small an atom is
description: An atom is on the order of a ten-billionth of a meter across: about 50 million in a row make a centimeter.

facts.text: An atom is on the order of one ten-billionth of a meter (0.1 nanometers) across.
About 50 million atoms of solid matter lined up in a row would measure about 1 centimeter.
A millimeter is ten million times the width of an atom 0.1 nanometers across.

title: The atom is mostly empty space
description: The nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller across than the atom: a blueberry in a football stadium. Electrons fill almost all the volume, yet the nucleus holds nearly all the mass.

facts.text: An atom's nucleus is about 100,000 times smaller across than the whole atom.
If an atom's nucleus were the size of a blueberry, the atom would be about the size of a football stadium.
An atom is mostly empty space: its electrons occupy almost all of its volume, around a tiny nucleus.

title: Electron shells
description: Electrons can sit only at certain energy levels, called shells (Bohr, 1913). The first shell holds up to 2 electrons and the second up to 8, and electrons fill the lowest-energy shell first.

facts.text: In 1913 Niels Bohr explained that electrons can exist only at certain allowed energy levels around the nucleus, now called shells.
The first electron shell holds up to 2 electrons, and the second holds up to 8.
Electrons fill the lowest-energy shell, closest to the nucleus, first; once a shell is full, the next electrons start a shell farther out.

title: The outer shell
description: Neon's 10 electrons fill two shells exactly; sodium's 11 are arranged 2, 8, 1. The outermost (valence) shell decides how an atom behaves chemically.

facts.text: Neon has 10 electrons, exactly enough to fill the first two shells.
Sodium's 11 electrons are arranged 2, 8, 1: two full shells and one electron in the third.
The outermost electron shell, the valence shell, determines an atom's chemical behavior.
With its shells full, neon is stable and rarely forms chemical bonds with other atoms.

title: Isotopes
description: Isotopes are atoms of one element (same protons) with different numbers of neutrons, and so different masses: carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14.

facts.text: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons, and so different masses.
An atom's mass number is its total count of protons and neutrons.
Carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 each have 6 protons, with 6, 7 and 8 neutrons.
About 99 percent of natural carbon is carbon-12 and about 1 percent is carbon-13; carbon-14 exists only in traces.
Hydrogen has three isotopes, each with 1 proton: ordinary hydrogen with no neutron, deuterium with 1 and tritium with 2.

title: Isotopes share their chemistry
description: Isotopes of an element behave almost identically in chemistry, because they have the same protons and electrons. Their name, Greek for "same place", dates from 1913.

facts.text: Isotopes of the same element have nearly identical chemical behavior.
In 1913 Margaret Todd suggested the name isotope, from Greek for "same place", to Frederick Soddy; isotopes share one place in the periodic table.

title: Radioactive decay
description: Unstable nuclei break down on their own, giving off radiation and sometimes becoming a different atom. Becquerel discovered it in 1896 when uranium salts fogged wrapped photographic plates without sunlight.

facts.text: In 1896 Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts gave off radiation that fogged photographic plates wrapped in opaque paper, even without sunlight.
When overcast skies spoiled his sunlight experiment in February 1896, Becquerel developed the plates anyway and found strong, clear images.
In radioactive decay, an unstable nucleus spontaneously breaks down toward a more stable one, giving off radiation.
Stable isotopes, left alone, show no tendency to change.
When a radioactive atom decays, it can turn into a different atom, called a decay product.

title: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation
description: Alpha particles are 2 protons and 2 neutrons (a helium nucleus), beta particles are small fast particles, often electrons, and gamma rays are high-energy photons.

facts.text: An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons: the nucleus of a helium atom.
A beta particle is a small, fast-moving particle, often an electron.
Gamma rays are packets of energy (photons): electromagnetic radiation in the same family as light and X-rays.

title: Half-life
description: A half-life is the time for half the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay. After two half-lives a quarter remain. Half-lives range from seconds to billions of years.

facts.text: A half-life is the time it takes for half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay.
After one half-life, half of the radioactive atoms remain; after two, a quarter; after three, an eighth.
Half-lives range from mere seconds to billions of years.

title: How carbon dating works
description: Cosmic rays make carbon-14 in the air; living things take it in through the food chain. After death the intake stops and carbon-14 decays with a half-life of about 5,730 years, so what remains tells the time since death.

facts.text: Carbon-14 forms in the atmosphere when neutrons produced by cosmic rays strike nitrogen-14.
Carbon-14 in the air's carbon dioxide is absorbed by green plants and passed on to animals through the food chain.
When an organism dies it stops taking in carbon-14, and the amount in its remains steadily drops as it decays to nitrogen-14.
Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years.
After about 11,460 years (two carbon-14 half-lives), about a quarter of the original carbon-14 remains.
Willard Libby developed radiocarbon dating in the late 1940s and won the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it.

title: What carbon dating can and cannot date
description: Carbon dating works only on once-living things, from about 500 to 50,000 years old. Dinosaurs are far too old.

facts.text: Carbon-14 dating works on once-living specimens from about 500 to 50,000 years old; older ones have too little carbon-14 left to measure.
Non-bird dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, more than 1,000 times older than carbon dating's 50,000-year reach.

title: Why light microscopes cannot see atoms
description: A light microscope cannot separate details closer than about half the wavelength of light, about 200 nanometers at best, a limit set by physics. Atoms are about 2,000 times smaller.

facts.text: A light microscope cannot separate details closer than about half the wavelength of light: about 200 nanometers at best.
This light-microscope limit is set by the physics of light itself, not by the quality of the lenses.
An atom 0.1 nanometers across is about 2,000 times smaller than the 200-nanometer limit of a light microscope.

title: The scanning tunneling microscope
description: The STM (Binnig and Rohrer, IBM, 1981) maps single atoms by scanning a one-atom-wide tip just above a surface and tracking a tunneling current. In 1989 it spelled IBM in 35 xenon atoms.

facts.text: Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer introduced the scanning tunneling microscope (STM) at IBM's Zurich lab in 1981.
Binnig and Rohrer received the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics for the scanning tunneling microscope.
An STM scans a needle whose tip narrows to a single atom, held about two atoms' width above the surface without touching it.
An STM's tip follows a surface much as a finger run along the tops of a row of books feels every change in height.
A small voltage lets electrons tunnel across the gap; the tip moves up or down to keep that current steady, and its path becomes a map of the surface.
An STM image shows the positions of atoms' electrons rather than a photograph of the atoms themselves.
In 1989 Don Eigler and Erhard Schweizer used an STM to spell IBM with 35 xenon atoms on a nickel surface.

title: Thomson finds the electron
description: In 1897 J.J. Thomson showed that cathode rays are particles far lighter than atoms, found in all matter: electrons. He pictured atoms as positive spheres with electrons embedded, the plum pudding model.

facts.text: In 1897 J.J. Thomson concluded that all matter contains particles much less massive than atoms: electrons.
Cathode rays occur when an electric current is driven through a tube with most of the air pumped out.
Thomson originally called electrons corpuscles.
Thomson's plum pudding model pictured the atom as a sphere of evenly spread positive matter with electrons embedded in it.

title: Rutherford finds the nucleus
description: In the gold foil experiment (1909), most alpha particles passed straight through but a very few bounced back. In 1911 Rutherford explained it with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus in mostly empty space.

facts.text: In 1909 Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, working with Ernest Rutherford, fired alpha particles at thin gold foil; most passed straight through, but a very few bounced almost straight back.
Rutherford said it was "almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you."
Alpha particles bouncing back off the foil contradicted Thomson's plum pudding model, with its evenly spread positive charge.
In 1911 Rutherford proposed that an atom's positive charge and nearly all its mass sit in a tiny nucleus, surrounded by electrons and mostly empty space.
James Chadwick found evidence of the neutron, an uncharged particle in the nucleus, in 1932.

title: The electron cloud
description: Electrons do not circle the nucleus like planets. Since Schrodinger (1926), they are described as waves occupying orbitals: regions where an electron is most likely to be found.

facts.text: Electrons do not circle the nucleus like planets around the Sun; they are found in regions called orbitals.
In 1926 Erwin Schrödinger described electrons in atoms as waves, laying the foundations of quantum wave mechanics.
An orbital is a region in an atom where an electron is most likely to be found.
In the quantum picture, a shell is a layer around the nucleus where its electrons are most likely to be found.

title: What an element is
description: An element is a pure substance that no chemical process can break down into simpler substances. Elements are the building blocks of all matter; compounds such as water are elements joined together. 118 are known.

facts.text: An element is a substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical processes.
Elements are the fundamental materials all matter is made of, and 118 chemical elements are known, the number on the IUPAC periodic table.
A compound is a pure substance made of two or more elements; water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen that can be broken down into them, yet its properties are altogether different from either.

title: Atomic number identifies an element
description: Every atom of an element has the same number of protons, its atomic number, and that number decides which element the atom is.

facts.text: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus is its atomic number, and it determines which element the atom is.
Hydrogen's atomic number is 1, oxygen's is 8 and gold's is 79.

title: How Mendeleev arranged the elements
description: In 1869 Mendeleev ordered the known elements by atomic weight and grouped those with similar properties, revealing a repeating pattern; Lothar Meyer found it independently. Today the order is by atomic number.

facts.text: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev published a table arranging the elements by increasing atomic weight, with elements of similar properties grouped together because their properties recurred in a pattern; Lothar Meyer in Germany independently published a similar table in 1870.
Today's periodic table orders the elements by atomic number rather than atomic weight; scientists recognized in the 1910s that atomic number is the true order.

title: Mendeleev's gaps and predictions
description: Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties; gallium, scandium and germanium later filled them, germanium matching closely.

facts.text: Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements not yet discovered and predicted their properties; gallium (1875), scandium (1879) and germanium (1886) were later found to fit.

For the missing element he called eka-silicon, Mendeleev predicted an atomic weight of 72, a gray color and a high melting point; Clemens Winkler found germanium in 1886, with an atomic weight of 72.6.

title: Groups and periods
description: The periodic table has 7 rows (periods) and 18 columns (groups). Properties recur along the rows (the periodic law), so elements in the same group behave alike.

facts.text: The periodic table has seven horizontal rows, called periods, and 18 vertical columns, called groups, with elements in order of atomic number.
Elements in the same group tend to behave in similar ways.
When the elements are arranged in order, their properties recur in a repeating pattern, called the periodic law, which gives the periodic table its name.

title: Reading an element's box and symbol
description: Each box shows an element's atomic number, symbol and name, usually with its atomic mass. Symbols are one or two letters; some come from Latin names.

facts.text: Each box on the periodic table shows an element's atomic number, symbol and name, usually with its atomic mass.

Element symbols are one or two letters with only the first capitalized (Co is cobalt, CO is carbon monoxide); some come from Latin names, such as Fe for iron (ferrum), Au for gold (aurum) and Pb for lead (plumbum).

title: Metals
description: About three-quarters of the elements are metals: shiny, malleable, ductile and good conductors of heat and electricity, and solid at room temperature except mercury.

facts.text: About three-quarters of the known chemical elements are metals.

Metals are lustrous (shiny), malleable (they can be hammered into thin sheets), ductile (they can be drawn into wire) and good conductors of heat and electricity; they are solid at room temperature except mercury.

title: Nonmetals, metalloids and the map
description: Nonmetals are dull, brittle when solid and poor conductors, and sit at the upper right; metalloids with in-between properties lie along the staircase line; mercury and bromine are the only liquid elements.

facts.text: Nonmetals tend to be dull, brittle when solid and poor conductors of heat and electricity; most are gases or solids at room temperature, and bromine is the only liquid one.
Metals fill the left side and middle of the periodic table, nonmetals the upper right, and metalloids, with properties between the two, lie along a staircase line between them.
At room temperature only two elements are liquids: mercury, a metal, and bromine, a deep-red nonmetal.

title: Noble gases
description: The group 18 noble gases barely react because their outer electron shells are complete; argon was found in air in 1894, and neon and argon are separated from liquid air.

facts.text: Lord Rayleigh and William Ramsay discovered argon in air in 1894; it makes up just under 1 percent of the atmosphere (about 0.94 percent), and its name comes from the Greek for idle or lazy.
The noble gases of group 18 are helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon and oganesson; they are colorless, odorless gases that very rarely form compounds.
Noble gases barely react because their outermost electron shells are complete.
Noble gases were long called inert, but in 1962 Neil Bartlett made a compound of xenon, showing they are not completely unreactive.
Neon and argon are obtained by fractional distillation of liquid air.

title: How neon lights glow
description: Electricity turns the gas in a neon tube into glowing plasma; neon glows reddish orange, and other colors come from other gases.

facts.text: Electricity passing through neon gas in a tube makes it glow reddish orange; only red signs contain actual neon, and other colors come from other gases such as argon and mercury.
Neon lights use electricity to turn the gas in the tube into glowing plasma.

title: The alkali metal family
description: Group 1 alkali metals (lithium to francium) are soft, silvery and so reactive they occur only in compounds; each has one outer electron it gives up easily.

facts.text: The alkali metals of group 1 are lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, cesium and francium; hydrogen sits at the top of group 1 but is not an alkali metal.
Alkali metals are soft, silvery metals; sodium can be cut with a knife at room temperature.
Alkali metals are so reactive that in nature they are found only in compounds, never as the pure metal; the sodium in seawater, for example, is mostly in dissolved sodium chloride.
Each alkali metal atom has a single electron in its outer shell, which it gives up easily; lower in the group that electron is farther from the nucleus and easier to remove.
Neon's atomic number is 10 and sodium's is 11.

title: Alkali metals and water
description: Alkali metals react with water to make hydrogen gas and a hydroxide (an alkali), releasing heat; the reaction grows more violent down the group.

facts.text: Alkali metals react with water to produce hydrogen gas and a metal hydroxide, a strong base (an alkali, which gives the group its name), releasing heat.

Alkali metals react more vigorously with water further down the group: lithium fizzes steadily, sodium melts into a ball that skims the surface, potassium gives off enough heat to ignite the hydrogen, rubidium reacts violently and cesium explodes.

title: The halogens
description: Group 17 halogens (fluorine to tennessine) are "salt formers": very reactive nonmetals one electron short of a full shell. Fluorine is the most reactive element; reactivity falls down the group. They range from gas to liquid to solid.

facts.text: The halogens of group 17 are fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine and tennessine; halogen means "salt former" in Greek, and with sodium they form salts, best known sodium chloride, table salt.
Halogens are very reactive nonmetals with seven outer electrons, one short of a full shell, and readily take one more; fluorine is the most reactive element, and reactivity decreases down the group.
At room temperature fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a deep-red liquid and iodine is a shiny black solid.
When warmed, solid iodine sublimes straight into a purple vapor; its name comes from the Greek for violet.

title: Halogens at work
description: Chlorine disinfects drinking water (routine in the US since Jersey City, 1908), fluorine compounds help prevent tooth decay, and iodide in salt prevents iodine deficiency.

facts.text: Chlorine, a toxic yellow-green gas named from the Greek chloros (greenish yellow), kills bacteria and is used to treat drinking water and swimming pool water.
In 1908 Jersey City, New Jersey, became the first US city to routinely disinfect its community drinking water; with disinfection and better sanitation, typhoid and cholera cases dropped dramatically.
Fluorine compounds help prevent tooth decay, and small amounts of iodide are added to table salt to prevent iodine deficiency.

title: Elements beyond uranium
description: Elements beyond uranium (92) are transuranium elements, all radioactive and made by people; neptunium, the first, was made in 1940.

facts.text: Elements beyond uranium (atomic number 92) are called transuranium elements; all 26 known are radioactive, all were first made artificially in nuclear reactors or particle accelerators, and only neptunium and plutonium occur in nature, in trace amounts.
In 1940 Edwin McMillan and Philip Abelson at Berkeley made element 93 by bombarding uranium with neutrons; they named it neptunium after Neptune, the first planet beyond Uranus.

title: Building superheavy elements
description: The heaviest elements are made by fusing nuclei in accelerators: element 118 came from calcium (20 protons) plus californium (98). IUPAC's 2016 names completed row seven.

facts.text: Element 118 was made at Dubna, Russia (runs in 2002 and 2005, reported in 2006), by a Russian and American team who fired calcium ions (20 protons) at a californium target (98 protons) at about 10 percent of the speed of light; fusion gave 118 protons.
Fusion of two nuclei is very rare: the element 118 experiments, runs in 2002 and 2005, produced three atoms in all.
In 2016 IUPAC named elements 113, 115, 117 and 118 nihonium, moscovium, tennessine and oganesson, completing the seventh row of the periodic table.
Oganesson is named after Yuri Oganessian (born 1933), a pioneer of superheavy element research who was alive when it was named; only a few atoms of oganesson have ever been made.

title: The Big Bang's elements
description: The Big Bang made all the hydrogen, most of the helium and some lithium: elements 1, 2 and 3. Nearly everything else was built later.

facts.text: The Big Bang made all of the hydrogen, most of the helium and some of the lithium in the universe; hydrogen, helium and lithium are elements 1, 2 and 3.

title: Stars forge the elements
description: Stars fuse lighter elements into heavier ones, such as carbon and oxygen, up to iron, and exploding stars scatter them into new stars, planets and people.

facts.text: Stars fuse lighter elements into heavier ones, such as helium into carbon and oxygen, up to iron.
When stars explode they blow their elements into space, where they become part of new stars and planets; carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and iron in our bodies were made in stars.

title: Where the heaviest natural elements came from
description: Fusion in stars stops at iron; heavier elements such as gold come from supernovas and neutron star mergers.

facts.text: Fusion in stars cannot make elements heavier than iron; those are made in supernova explosions and in collisions of neutron stars, the ultra-dense remains of dead stars.
In 2017 telescopes observed a neutron star merger that could have created gold, platinum and other heavy elements.

title: Reading behavior from position
description: Metallic character is strongest at the left and increases down a group, so the most metallic elements are at the lower left and nonmetallic character peaks at the upper right; an element's position predicts how it behaves.

facts.text: Metallic character is strongest at the left of the periodic table and increases down a group, so the most metallic elements sit at the lower left, while nonmetallic character is strongest at the upper right.

title: Hydrogen, the universe's most common element
description: Hydrogen is the simplest and most abundant element in the universe: more than 90 percent of all atoms and about three-quarters of ordinary matter by mass.

facts.text: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe: more than 90 percent of all atoms and about three-quarters of the mass of ordinary matter.
Hydrogen is the simplest of the chemical elements, and it is about three times as abundant as helium, the next most common element in the universe.

title: Hydrogen, the lightest gas
description: Hydrogen gas is the lightest of all gases, about 14 times less dense than air, so it rises fast and can escape from the top of Earth's atmosphere.

facts.text: Hydrogen is the lightest of all gases, about 14 times less dense than air, and it rises through air very quickly.
Free hydrogen gas is scarce in Earth's air because its light molecules move fast enough to escape from the top of the atmosphere into space.

title: Hydrogen, the water maker
description: On Earth most hydrogen is bound in water. Cavendish showed in 1766 that it is a distinct substance; it burns with oxygen to form water, hence Lavoisier's name, meaning maker of water.

facts.text: On Earth, hydrogen occurs in vast amounts as part of the water in oceans, ice, rivers and lakes.
In 1766 Henry Cavendish showed that hydrogen, a gas that burns, is a distinct substance.
Hydrogen burns with oxygen to form water, and Lavoisier named it from Greek words meaning maker of water.

title: How much oxygen there is
description: Oxygen makes up 21 percent of the air by volume and is the most plentiful element in Earth's crust, nearly half of it by weight, bound up in rocks.

facts.text: Oxygen makes up 21 percent of the atmosphere by volume.
Oxygen is the most plentiful element in Earth's crust, nearly half of it by weight (Britannica gives 46 percent), bound up in rocks.

title: Oxygen feeds flames and cells
description: Oxygen reacts with practically every element. Burning usually combines a fuel with oxygen, and cells combine oxygen with food molecules to release energy.

facts.text: Oxygen forms compounds by reacting with practically every other element.
Burning (combustion) is a chemical reaction that usually combines a fuel with oxygen from the air, giving off heat and light and forming products such as carbon dioxide and water.
Your cells combine oxygen with food molecules to release energy, giving off carbon dioxide and water.
In 1774 Joseph Priestley made a gas in which a candle burned more vigorously and a mouse thrived: oxygen.

title: Discovering and naming oxygen
description: Scheele (about 1772) and Priestley (1774) discovered oxygen independently. Lavoisier named it acid former, wrongly believing all acids contain it; the name stuck.

facts.text: Carl Wilhelm Scheele discovered oxygen about 1772, and Joseph Priestley discovered it independently in 1774.
Lavoisier named oxygen from Greek words meaning acid former, because he believed every acid contained it; acids without oxygen, such as hydrochloric acid, were found later, but the name stuck.

title: Carbon links to four atoms
description: A carbon atom can form up to four strong bonds, including bonds to other carbon atoms, so carbon builds chains, branched chains and rings of many sizes.

facts.text: A carbon atom can form up to four strong bonds, including bonds to other carbon atoms, giving chains, branched chains and rings of many sizes and shapes.

title: Carbon's enormous family of compounds
description: Carbon is only a trace in Earth's crust, yet it forms more compounds than all other elements combined: many millions known, and perhaps 10^60 possible.

facts.text: Carbon makes up only a few hundredths of a percent of Earth's crust, yet it forms more compounds than all the other elements combined.
Many millions of carbon compounds are known, and the number of possible organic compounds has been estimated at 10^60 (a 1 followed by 60 zeros).
Organic (carbon) compounds are key parts of plastics, soaps, perfumes, fabrics and medicines.

title: Carbon, the element of life
description: All living things are made mostly of carbon compounds. Organic molecules have carbon as their main element, bonded to hydrogen and other carbon atoms.

facts.text: All living things on Earth are made mostly of carbon compounds; carbon is essential to life because it forms extensive networks of bonds with itself and other elements.
Organic molecules have carbon as their principal element, bonded to hydrogen and other carbon atoms; their study is organic chemistry.

title: Diamond and graphite: one element, two forms
description: Diamond and graphite are the two most common allotropes of carbon: both pure carbon, with the atoms arranged differently.

facts.text: Diamond and graphite are the two most common allotropes (forms) of carbon: both are pure carbon, with their atoms arranged differently.

title: Why diamond is so hard
description: In diamond every carbon atom is bonded to four others in a three-dimensional network, making it the hardest known natural substance. Diamonds form deep in the mantle.

facts.text: In diamond every carbon atom is bonded to four other carbon atoms in a three-dimensional network, and this structure makes diamond the hardest known natural substance.
Diamonds form in Earth's mantle more than 120 km down, where temperatures and pressures are immense, and volcanic eruptions carry them toward the surface.

title: Why graphite is soft and slippery
description: Graphite's carbon atoms lie in flat sheets of hexagons held together only weakly, so the sheets slide apart: soft, good for pencils, and able to conduct electricity.

facts.text: In graphite, carbon atoms lie in flat layers of linked hexagons; the forces between layers are weak, so the layers slide easily, making graphite soft and slippery.
Graphite conducts electricity, while diamond does not.
At room temperature and normal pressure graphite is more stable than diamond, but diamond changes to graphite so slowly that a diamond lasts indefinitely.
Pencil lead is graphite mixed with clay and contains no lead; graphite found at Borrowdale, England, in 1564 was thought to be lead until Scheele showed in 1779 that it is carbon.
The name graphite comes from the Greek graphein, to write.

title: Iron: the planet's metal
description: Iron is the most abundant element in Earth as a whole (about 35 percent), mostly in the core; it is fourth in the crust and the most-used, cheapest metal.

facts.text: Iron is the most abundant element in Earth as a whole, about 35 percent, and the chief ingredient of Earth's core.
In Earth's crust iron is fourth in abundance, about 5 percent, after oxygen, silicon and aluminum.
Iron is the most-used and cheapest metal.

title: Steel: iron plus a little carbon
description: Pure iron is soft. Steel is iron with up to about 2 percent carbon, far harder and the world's main building material; cast iron, with 2 to 4 percent carbon, is brittle.

facts.text: Pure iron is relatively soft; adding carbon, up to about 2 percent, makes steel, which is far harder and by far the most widely used material for building the world's infrastructure.
Cast iron contains 2 to 4 percent carbon and is brittle and weak when pulled.

title: Iron in your blood
description: Most of the body's iron is in hemoglobin, the blood protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body.

facts.text: Most of the iron in your body is in hemoglobin, the protein in blood that carries oxygen from the lungs throughout the body.

title: Gold ignores oxygen and sulfur
description: Gold is one of the least reactive metals: unaffected by oxygen or sulfur, it never corrodes or tarnishes, is found fairly pure in nature, and is the most malleable element.

facts.text: Gold does not corrode or tarnish: it is one of the least reactive metals and is not affected by oxygen or sulfur.
Gold is usually found in nature in fairly pure form, for example as nuggets.
Gold is the most malleable element: one ounce can be beaten into a sheet of about 300 square feet.

title: Gold and silver as money
description: Some of the earliest coins, from Lydia, used electrum, a natural gold-silver mix; King Croesus switched to pure gold and silver coins.

facts.text: Some of the earliest coins, Lydian staters from around the second half of the 7th century BCE, were made of electrum, a naturally occurring gold-silver alloy.
King Croesus of Lydia replaced electrum coins with highly pure gold and silver coins, whose worth was easier to calculate than electrum's mix of metals.

title: Silver: best conductor, easy tarnish
description: Silver has the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of all metals, but sulfur compounds in air tarnish it with a dark coating.

facts.text: Silver has the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of all metals.
Silver tarnishes when exposed to sulfur or sulfur compounds in the air, forming a dark coating of silver sulfide.

title: Copper, the first metal
description: Copper occurs as free metal, so it was one of the first metals people used, around 8000 BCE. It is second only to silver as a conductor and mostly goes into electrical uses.

facts.text: Copper is found in nature as a free metal, and Neolithic people first used native copper in place of stone around 8000 BCE, about 10,000 years ago.
Copper is second only to silver in electrical conductivity, and electrical industries use most of the copper produced.

title: Bronze: copper plus tin
description: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, first made deliberately about 3500 BCE. It is harder than copper and melts more readily, so it casts well; bell metal has extra tin.

facts.text: Bronze is an alloy (a mixture) of copper and tin; metalworkers began deliberately alloying copper with tin around 3500 BCE.
Bronze is harder than copper, and it melts more readily, so it is easier to cast.
Modern bronze is typically about 88 percent copper and 12 percent tin; bell metal, a bronze with 20–25 percent tin, rings when struck.

title: The Bronze Age
description: The Bronze Age saw the first widespread use of metal, bronze, for tools and weapons; from about 1000 BCE iron working brought it to an end.

facts.text: The Bronze Age saw the first widespread use of metal, in the form of bronze, for tools and weapons.
Around 1000 BCE, the ability to heat and forge iron brought the Bronze Age to an end, and the Iron Age began.

title: Aluminum: plentiful but locked away
description: Aluminum is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust, about 8 percent, but it is so chemically active that it never occurs as a metal in nature. It is about one-third as dense as iron or copper.

facts.text: Aluminum is the most abundant metal in Earth's crust, about 8 percent by weight; only oxygen and silicon are more plentiful.
Because it is chemically active, aluminum never occurs as a metal in nature; it is locked in compounds in rocks.
Aluminum is only about one-third as dense as iron or copper.

title: When aluminum outshone gold
description: In the mid-1800s aluminum was more valuable than gold; Napoleon III gave his most important guests aluminum cutlery while others ate with silver.

facts.text: In the mid-1800s aluminum was more valuable than gold.
Napoleon III gave his most important guests aluminum cutlery, while less important guests dined with silver.

title: 1886: electricity frees aluminum
description: In 1886 Hall and Heroult independently found how to make aluminum by electrolysis of alumina dissolved in molten cryolite; by 1891 it cost under $1 a pound.

facts.text: In 1886 Charles Martin Hall in the United States and Paul Heroult in France independently found how to make aluminum by passing electricity through purified alumina (aluminum oxide) dissolved in molten cryolite.
Hall did his experiments partly in his college lab and partly in his family's woodshed.
After the new process, the price of aluminum fell below $1 a pound by 1891, and it became a common metal for things like cooking utensils and aircraft.

title: Silicon: the crust's second element
description: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, more than a quarter of it by weight. It never occurs free, but combined with oxygen as silica in rocks and sand.

facts.text: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust after oxygen, more than a quarter of it by weight.
Silicon is never found free in nature; it occurs in practically all rocks, sand, clays and soils, combined with oxygen as silica in minerals such as quartz.

title: Silicon, the tunable semiconductor
description: Silicon is a semiconductor, between a conductor and an insulator. Doping it with about 10 boron atoms per million raises its conductivity about a thousandfold.

facts.text: Silicon is a semiconductor: a solid whose electrical conductivity lies between that of a conductor and an insulator.
Adding about 10 boron atoms per million silicon atoms, a process called doping, can raise silicon's electrical conductivity a thousandfold (about 1,000 times).

title: Silicon chips
description: Doped silicon makes transistors, tiny switches that computer chips are built from. Chip silicon must be extremely pure, with fewer than 1 stray atom per 10 billion.

facts.text: Transistors are semiconductor devices that work as switches, turning electric current on and off; computer chips are built from them, mostly in silicon.
Silicon has become by far the most widely used semiconductor, virtually replacing germanium.
Silicon for electronics must be extremely pure, with fewer than 1 dopant atom per 10 billion silicon atoms.

title: The elements inside a phone
description: Old phones hold recoverable metals: a million recycled phones can yield about 35 thousand pounds of copper, 772 pounds of silver and 75 pounds of gold. Gold plates contacts because it conducts well and never tarnishes.

facts.text: Recycling a million cell phones can recover about 35 thousand pounds of copper, 772 pounds of silver, 75 pounds of gold and 33 pounds of palladium.
Because gold conducts electricity well and does not react, it is used to plate electrical contacts, terminals and printed circuits.

title: What a molecule is
description: A molecule is two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds: the smallest piece of a pure substance that is still that substance. Split a water molecule and you get hydrogen and oxygen, not smaller water.

facts.text: A molecule is a group of two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds; it is the smallest unit into which a pure substance can be divided and still keep its makeup and chemical properties.
When water molecules are broken apart, the pieces are hydrogen and oxygen, gases whose makeup and properties differ from water's.

title: A molecule's fixed recipe
description: Every water molecule holds exactly two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom; that fixed makeup separates a compound from a mixture. Some molecules pair identical atoms, like the oxygen and nitrogen in air.

facts.text: Every water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom; this fixed makeup distinguishes a chemical compound from a mixture, whose makeup can vary.
Most samples of the elements hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen are made of molecules containing two atoms each, called diatomic molecules, with the formulas H2, O2 and N2.

title: Water, a polar molecule
description: Oxygen pulls water's shared electrons harder than hydrogen does, so the oxygen end is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends slightly positive. The hydrogens sit at an angle of about 104.5°, so the molecule is polar.

facts.text: In a water molecule, oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen does, so the oxygen end has a slight negative charge and the hydrogen ends slight positive charges.
The two hydrogen atoms in a water molecule are attached to the oxygen at an angle of about 104.5°, not in a straight line.

title: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules
description: The slightly positive hydrogen of one water molecule is drawn to the oxygen of its neighbor: a hydrogen bond. Breaking these is why water boils at 100 °C instead of about −80 °C; they also give water surface tension and hold ice's open lattice.

facts.text: The slightly positive hydrogen of one water molecule is attracted to the oxygen of a neighboring molecule; this attraction between molecules is called a hydrogen bond.
Hydrogen bonds are attractions between molecules, and they are much weaker than the covalent bonds that hold the atoms together inside a molecule.
Following the trend of similar compounds such as hydrogen sulfide, water would be expected to boil at about −80 °C; hydrogen bonding is why it actually boils at 100 °C.
Because water molecules attract one another, water's surface behaves like a skin: this surface tension lets water striders walk on it and can float a steel paper clip.
When water freezes, hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open lattice that holds them farther apart than in the liquid, which is why ice is less dense than liquid water.

title: Ionic bonds: a trade of electrons
description: In table salt, each sodium atom gives one electron to a chlorine atom, making a positive sodium ion and a negative chloride ion. The attraction between opposite charges is the ionic bond.

facts.text: Table salt, sodium chloride, is made from sodium, a soft, silvery-white metal that burns vigorously in air, and chlorine, a yellow-green gas that is very poisonous.
In sodium chloride, each sodium atom gives one electron to a chlorine atom; atoms that lose or gain electrons become charged ions, here positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions.
An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

title: Salt: a grid of ions, not molecules
description: Sodium chloride has no molecules: its ions form a three-dimensional grid, each surrounded by six of the opposite charge. It melts only at 801 °C, but water pulls its ions apart when it dissolves.

facts.text: Sodium chloride is not made of molecules: its ions form a three-dimensional lattice in which each ion is surrounded by six ions of the opposite charge.
Ionic compounds typically melt at high temperatures: sodium chloride melts at 801 °C.
When salt dissolves, polar water molecules surround the ions and pull the sodium and chloride ions apart.

title: Covalent bonds: sharing electrons
description: A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms. Identical atoms share equally; different atoms share unequally, making a polar bond. Hydrogen, nitrogen, water and all organic compounds are held this way.

facts.text: A covalent bond forms when two atoms share a pair of electrons between them.
Identical atoms, as in a hydrogen molecule, share their bonding electrons equally; different atoms share them unequally, which makes the bond polar.
Molecules held together by covalent bonds include hydrogen, nitrogen, water and all organic compounds.

title: Single, double and triple bonds
description: Atoms can share one, two or three pairs of electrons. Hydrogen has a single bond, oxygen gas a double bond and nitrogen gas a triple bond, so strong that nitrogen, about 78 percent of the air, barely reacts.

facts.text: Atoms can share one, two or three pairs of electrons, forming single, double or triple bonds: hydrogen molecules have a single bond, oxygen a double bond and nitrogen a triple bond.
About 78 percent of the air is nitrogen gas, whose two atoms are joined by a very strong triple bond, which makes nitrogen gas very unreactive.

title: Strong inside, loose outside
description: Covalent bonds inside a molecule are strong, but the pulls between molecules are much weaker, so covalent substances melt and boil far lower than ionic ones. Melting or boiling water separates whole molecules; the bonds inside stay intact.

facts.text: Covalent (molecular) compounds generally melt and boil at much lower temperatures than ionic compounds; many are liquids or gases at room temperature.
When a molecular substance such as water melts or boils, only the attractions between molecules are overcome; the covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact.

title: Metallic bonds: a sea of electrons
description: In a metal, atoms pack tightly and their outer electrons roam freely through the whole piece, a sea of electrons around positive ions. The attraction between the ions and that shared sea is the metallic bond.

facts.text: In a metal, the atoms are packed closely and their outer electrons are not tied to any one atom: they wander freely through the whole piece, a sea of electrons around positive metal ions, and the attraction between the ions and this sea holds the metal together.

title: Why metals conduct and bend
description: Free electrons let metals conduct electricity; solid salt can't, because its ions are locked in place. Hammered, a metal's layers slide while the electron sea keeps them bonded, but a salt crystal's shifted layers push like charges together and it shatters.

facts.text: Metals conduct electricity well because their free electrons can move through the metal.
Solid ionic compounds like salt do not conduct electricity because their ions are fixed in place; melted or dissolved, the ions can move and they conduct.
Metals are malleable: when hammered, their layers of ions slide past one another while the sea of electrons shifts with them and keeps them bonded, so the metal deforms instead of breaking.
Ionic solids are hard and brittle: when a blow shifts their layers, ions of the same charge are pushed side by side and repel, and the crystal shatters.

title: What makes a crystal
description: A crystal is a solid whose particles sit in a pattern that repeats in every direction, and its outside often shows it: salt grains are cubes, and snowflakes have six-fold symmetry from ice's hexagonal arrangement.

facts.text: A crystal is a solid whose atoms, ions or molecules are arranged in a definite pattern that repeats in all directions; its outer regularity reflects that inner order.
Salt crystals are cubic, reflecting the cubic arrangement of sodium and chloride ions inside them.
The six-fold symmetry of a snowflake comes from the hexagonal arrangement of water molecules in the ice crystal lattice.

title: How crystals grow
description: Crystals grow as particles join the pattern, from a solution, a cooling melt or a vapor (frost). Slow growth makes larger crystals: Naica's 11-meter gypsum crystals grew for hundreds of thousands of years in water at a steady temperature.

facts.text: Crystals grow as particles join an ordered pattern, from a solution, from a vapor or from a cooling melt.
Slow crystallization encourages larger crystals, while crystals that form quickly are smaller.
In 2000, miners in Naica, Mexico, broke into a cave of gypsum crystals up to about 11 meters long.
Naica's crystals grew slowly in hot, mineral-rich water that stayed in a narrow, stable temperature range for many hundreds of thousands of years.

title: Polymers: molecules as chains
description: A polymer is a giant molecule built from many small repeating units (monomers). Polyethylene, the most widely used plastic, is ethylene linked into long chains, and chain length and arrangement make plastics strong, light and flexible.

facts.text: A polymer is a substance made of very large molecules, each built from many small repeating units called monomers.
The word polymer means "of many parts."
Polyethylene, the most widely used plastic in the world, is made by linking ethylene molecules into long chains; it is used in food wrap, shopping bags and detergent bottles.
The length of polymer chains and the patterns in which they are arranged make plastics strong, lightweight and flexible.

title: Nature's polymers
description: Living things are full of polymers: cellulose, starch, proteins, natural rubber and DNA. DNA's links come in four kinds (A, C, G, T); the human genome is about 3 billion bases, and one cell's DNA would stretch about 6 feet.

facts.text: Nature makes polymers too: cellulose in plant cell walls, starch, proteins, natural rubber and nucleic acids such as DNA.
DNA is a chain of building blocks called nucleotides whose bases come in four kinds (A, C, G and T); the human genome contains about 3 billion bases.
If all the DNA molecules in a single human cell were unwound and placed end to end, they would stretch about 6 feet (about 1.8 meters).

title: Reading a chemical formula
description: A formula names each kind of atom by its symbol and counts it with a subscript; no subscript means one. H2O is two hydrogens and one oxygen; CO2 is one carbon and two oxygens.

facts.text: A molecular formula uses element symbols for the kinds of atoms and subscripts for how many of each; with no subscript, there is one atom.
Water's formula is H2O (two hydrogen atoms, one oxygen atom) and carbon dioxide's is CO2 (one carbon atom, two oxygen atoms).

title: One atom changes the substance
description: Change one count and you change the substance: O2 is the oxygen you breathe, O3 is ozone, an irritating toxic gas; H2O is water, H2O2 is a bleach and antiseptic. Salt's formula NaCl is a ratio of ions, not a molecule.

facts.text: Ozone, O3, has three oxygen atoms instead of the two in ordinary oxygen gas (O2); it is a pale blue, irritating, toxic gas, and high in the atmosphere it absorbs the Sun's ultraviolet radiation.
Hydrogen peroxide, H2O2, is a colorless liquid used as a bleach and as an antiseptic.
For an ionic compound like sodium chloride, the formula NaCl gives the ratio of its ions (one sodium ion for each chloride ion), not a molecule; chemists call it a formula unit.

title: Electron pairs set a molecule's shape
description: Around a central atom, electron pairs repel and spread as far apart as possible, which sets the molecule's shape: methane's four hydrogens point to the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart.

facts.text: Electron pairs around a central atom, whether in bonds or not, repel one another and spread as far apart as possible; this sets the molecule's shape.
In methane, the four hydrogen atoms around the carbon spread into a tetrahedral shape, with bond angles of 109.5°.

title: Why a molecule's shape matters
description: Shape decides behavior. Straight CO2's polar bonds cancel, so it is nonpolar; bent water's don't, so it is polar. Carvone's two mirror-image forms smell of spearmint and caraway because each fits different receptors in the nose.

facts.text: Carbon dioxide is a straight (linear) molecule: each of its two bonds is polar, but they point in opposite directions and cancel, so the molecule as a whole is nonpolar.
Water is bent because of the unshared electron pairs on its oxygen atom, so its two polar bonds do not cancel and the molecule is polar.

Carvone comes in two mirror-image forms: spearmint plants make one and caraway plants the other, and they smell different because odor receptors in the nose are themselves chiral (handed), so each form fits different receptors.

title: Reading bonds from properties
description: A solid's properties hint at its bonding: ionic solids are hard, brittle, high-melting and conduct only melted or dissolved; metals conduct as solids and bend; molecular substances are often gases, liquids or low-melting solids.

facts.text: A substance's properties hint at its bonding: ionic solids are hard, brittle and high-melting; metals conduct electricity as solids and bend; molecular substances are often gases, liquids or low-melting solids.

title: Reactants and products
description: In a chemical reaction, the starting substances (reactants) turn into new substances (products). Chemists write reactants on the left of an arrow and products on the right. Burning wood: wood and oxygen become carbon dioxide, water vapor and ash.

facts.text: In a chemical reaction, the starting substances, the reactants, are converted into different substances, the products; in an equation, reactants are written to the left of an arrow and products to the right.
When wood burns, wood and oxygen are transformed into carbon dioxide, water vapor and ash.
Hydrogen is a flammable gas that burns with oxygen to form water, a compound with entirely different properties that does not burn and is used to put out fires.

title: Reactions rearrange atoms
description: A reaction breaks the bonds holding the reactants together and reassembles the same atoms into new combinations, so no atoms are made or destroyed; only their arrangement changes.

facts.text: A chemical reaction rearranges the atoms of the reactants: bonds in the reactants break and the atoms are reassembled into products by forming new bonds, with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.

title: Conservation of mass in reactions
description: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. When products seem lighter or heavier, matter has slipped in or out unseen, usually as a gas: ash is light because gases escape, and a metal gets heavier as it combines with oxygen.

facts.text: In a chemical reaction, matter is neither created nor destroyed: the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants, even when some of them are invisible gases.
The ash left by burning wood weighs far less than the wood because most of the mass leaves as carbon dioxide and water vapor; the ash plus the gases weigh as much as the wood plus the oxygen it used.
A metal gets heavier when it combines with oxygen, because the oxygen's mass is added; Lavoisier measured the weight gained when elements were oxidized.

title: Lavoisier's sealed-vessel experiment
description: Antoine Lavoisier, an 18th-century French chemist, weighed everything in his reactions. He heated tin sealed in a vessel with air: the solid gained exactly as much mass as the air lost, so the total stayed the same.

facts.text: Antoine Lavoisier (1743 to 1794), a French chemist, made a point of collecting and weighing all the substances involved in the reactions he studied.
Lavoisier sealed tin in a vessel with air, heated it and weighed it: the solids (tin plus a powder) gained exactly as much mass as the air inside lost, so the total mass did not change.

title: Combustion
description: Burning (combustion) is a reaction between a fuel and oxygen that gives off heat and usually light. Fuels made of carbon and hydrogen burn mainly to carbon dioxide and water; with too little oxygen they can make toxic carbon monoxide. In a candle, it is the wax vapor that burns.

facts.text: Combustion, or burning, is a chemical reaction between a fuel and oxygen, usually accompanied by heat and light in the form of flame.
When fuels containing carbon and hydrogen burn completely, the main products are carbon dioxide and water; methane burning in oxygen, for example, gives carbon dioxide and water.
Incomplete burning of carbon-containing fuels can produce carbon monoxide, an odorless, colorless, toxic gas.
In a burning candle, the flame's heat melts the wax and turns it into vapor, and it is the wax vapor mixing with oxygen that burns; the heat released keeps producing more vapor.

title: The fire triangle
description: A fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat at once. Remove any one and it goes out: water removes heat, smothering removes oxygen, a firebreak removes fuel.

facts.text: A fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen, the fire triangle; remove any one and it goes out: water removes heat, smothering (stop, drop and roll) removes oxygen, and a cleared fireline removes fuel.

title: How iron rusts
description: Rust is reddish-brown iron oxide. Iron rusts when it meets oxygen and water together, and salts speed it up. Because oxygen joins the iron, rust weighs more than the iron it came from.

facts.text: Rust is a reddish-brown iron oxide that forms when iron is exposed to oxygen and water together.
Salts and acids speed up the rusting of iron.

title: Why rust spreads, and how to stop it
description: Unlike copper's protective coat, rust flakes off and exposes fresh iron, so corrosion keeps going. Paint blocks oxygen and water; galvanizing coats iron with zinc, which corrodes first.

facts.text: Unlike copper, which forms a protective coating, iron's rust does not protect it: the rust flakes off and exposes fresh iron to the air, so corrosion continues.
Paint protects iron by keeping oxygen and water away, and galvanizing coats iron with zinc, a metal that oxidizes more readily, so the zinc corrodes instead of the iron.

title: Reactions need good collisions
description: Particles react only when they collide in the right orientation and with at least a minimum energy, the activation energy. Anything that makes such collisions more frequent speeds a reaction up.

facts.text: Particles react only when they collide in a suitable orientation and with enough energy; the minimum energy needed is called the activation energy.

title: Temperature and reaction speed
description: Reactions usually go faster when warmer: particles move faster, collide more often and more of them clear the activation energy. For many reactions, 10 °C roughly doubles the rate. A fridge slows spoiling.

facts.text: Chemical reactions typically go faster at higher temperatures, because more particles have enough energy to react; for many reactions the rate roughly doubles for a 10 °C rise.
Food can spoil quickly on a kitchen counter, but the lower temperature inside a refrigerator slows that process so the same food stays fresh for days.

title: Surface area, concentration and reaction speed
description: A solid reacts only at its surface, so smaller pieces react faster: a log smolders, sawdust burns explosively. Higher concentrations of reactants usually speed reactions up too.

facts.text: A reaction involving a solid happens only at its surface, so smaller pieces with more exposed surface react faster: large pieces of wood smolder, smaller pieces burn rapidly and sawdust burns explosively.
Reaction rates usually increase when the concentration of one or more reactants increases.

title: Catalysts
description: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up, so it can keep working. Berzelius named the effect catalysis in 1835. Substances in a wound make hydrogen peroxide foam as it rapidly breaks down.

facts.text: A catalyst is a substance that speeds up a reaction without being consumed by it.
The Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius coined the word catalysis in 1835, from Greek words meaning to loosen down.
Dilute hydrogen peroxide breaks down slowly on its own, but on an open wound it breaks down rapidly and foams, releasing oxygen gas, because substances in the tissue act as catalysts.

title: How catalysts work
description: A catalyst opens a different route for a reaction with a lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed. It does not change the reactants or products.

facts.text: A catalyst works by providing a different route for the reaction with a lower activation energy, without changing the overall reaction.

title: Catalytic converters
description: Gasoline cars carry catalytic converters in which metals such as platinum and rhodium turn carbon monoxide, unburned fuel and nitrogen oxides into carbon dioxide, water vapor, nitrogen and oxygen.

facts.text: Modern cars use three-way catalytic converters, in which platinum and rhodium catalysts turn carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide and water vapor, and nitrogen oxides into nitrogen and oxygen.

title: Exothermic and endothermic
description: An exothermic change releases heat (fire, a hand warmer rusting iron powder); an endothermic change absorbs heat (an instant cold pack).

facts.text: A change that releases heat is exothermic; a change that absorbs heat is endothermic.
Combustion is exothermic: burning fuel releases energy as heat, and often light.
Air-activated hand warmers contain iron powder, salt and water; once unwrapped, oxygen reacts with the iron to form iron oxide (rust) and release heat, and more iron surface area means more reaction.
An instant cold pack for muscle strains is endothermic: when the water and the salt inside are brought together, the process absorbs heat.

title: Where reaction energy comes from
description: Breaking bonds takes energy in; forming bonds gives energy out. A reaction is exothermic when the new bonds release more energy than breaking the old ones took, and endothermic when it is the other way round.

facts.text: Energy is absorbed to break bonds and released when bonds form; a reaction is exothermic when forming the products' bonds releases more energy than breaking the reactants' bonds took, and endothermic otherwise.

title: Firework colors come from metals
description: Fireworks began more than a thousand years ago, most likely in China, and were long only orange. In the 1800s chemists added compounds for color: strontium red, barium green, copper blue, sodium yellow. Blue is the hardest.

facts.text: Fireworks trace back more than 1,000 years, most likely to China; for centuries they glowed only orange and gold, like the glow of very hot particles.
In the 1800s, chemists began burning newly made compounds in fireworks to produce red, green, blue and purple.
In fireworks, strontium produces red, barium green, copper blue and sodium yellow; copper and strontium together make lavender.
Blue is the most difficult firework color to produce; over recent decades it has improved from an anemic bluish white to a true azure.

title: Why each metal glows its own color
description: The heat of the burning firework gives electrons in the metal atoms extra energy; as they drop back they release light, and the size of the drop, which differs for each element, sets the color.

facts.text: In a firework, heat gives electrons in the metal atoms extra energy; as they fall back they release it as light, and the size of the energy drop, different for each element, sets the color.

title: What an explosion is
description: An explosion is a rapid release of energy that makes a large volume of expanding gas in a very short time. Many are combustion sped up: the difference from a fire is speed.

facts.text: An explosion is a rapid release of energy that produces a large volume of expanding gas in a very short time.
Combustion turns into an explosion when the reaction accelerates, for example as its temperature rises.

title: Deflagration and detonation
description: In a deflagration the reaction moves through the material slower than sound (gunpowder, a low explosive, burns this way). In a detonation a supersonic shock wave sets the material off as it goes (high explosives).

facts.text: Low explosives such as gunpowder burn rapidly (deflagrate) with the reaction moving slower than sound; high explosives detonate, with a shock wave moving faster than sound setting off the material.

title: Dust explosions
description: Ordinary combustible materials like sugar, flour or wood can burn rapidly when finely divided and explode when the dust hangs in air, because every grain is exposed. A 2008 sugar dust explosion in Georgia killed 14 workers.

facts.text: Combustible materials burn rapidly when finely divided and can explode when the dust is suspended in air; sugar, flour, wood, coal and metals such as aluminum are among them.
In 2008, a sugar dust explosion at a refinery in Port Wentworth, Georgia, killed 14 workers.

title: Oxidation at different speeds
description: Rusting and burning are both oxidation, originally meaning combining with oxygen. They differ in speed: rust creeps, fire races, an explosion is faster still.

facts.text: Oxidation originally meant a substance combining with oxygen; rusting and burning are both oxidation reactions, rusting slow and burning fast.

title: What makes an acid
description: Acids taste sour (the word comes from Latin for sour) and, in water, hand off hydrogen ions (protons): lemons, vinegar and stomach acid all contain acids.

facts.text: The word acid comes from the Latin acidus, meaning sour or sharp.
Acids taste sour: lemons and other citrus fruits contain citric acid, vinegar contains acetic acid, and the stomach produces hydrochloric acid.
Tasting or touching chemicals is not good laboratory practice; chemists identify acids and bases with tests instead.
In water an acid releases positively charged hydrogen ions (H+); a hydrogen ion is essentially a bare proton, so an acid is also called a proton donor.

title: Strong and weak acids
description: A strong acid such as hydrochloric acid ionizes almost completely in water; a weak acid such as the acetic acid in vinegar ionizes only a little.

facts.text: A strong acid such as hydrochloric acid ionizes essentially completely in water; a weak acid such as acetic acid ionizes only partly, about 1.3 percent in a 0.100 M solution.
Vinegar is a dilute solution of acetic acid in water, about 5 percent acetic acid by volume.

title: What makes a base
description: Bases taste bitter and feel slippery; soap, baking soda, ammonia cleaners and lye are bases. A base accepts hydrogen ions, often by releasing hydroxide ions into water.

facts.text: Bases often taste bitter and feel slippery; soaps contain bases, ammonia is a base used in cleaners and sodium hydroxide (lye) is in drain cleaners.
Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate (sodium hydrogen carbonate), a mildly alkaline compound also used as an antacid.
A base accepts hydrogen ions (it is a proton acceptor); many bases, such as sodium hydroxide, do this by releasing hydroxide ions (OH-) into water.

title: Alkalis, from plant ashes
