description: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, such as sodium or potassium hydroxide. The word first meant plant ashes; strong alkalis are caustic.

facts.text: The word alkali comes, through Medieval Latin, from Arabic al-qili, the ashes of the saltwort plant; it was first applied to the ashes of burned plants.

Alkalis are bases that dissolve in water, such as sodium hydroxide (lye) and potassium hydroxide; they were once leached from plant ashes, react with fats or oils to make soap, and are caustic to skin and tissue.

title: The pH scale
description: pH, introduced by Sorensen in 1909, puts acidity on one scale, usually 0 to 14: 7 is neutral, lower is acidic, higher is basic. More hydrogen ions mean a lower pH.

facts.text: In 1909 the Danish chemist S.P.L. Sorensen, head of chemistry at the Carlsberg Laboratory (backed by the beer company), introduced pH; before it there was no widely accepted way to express acidity.
The pH scale usually runs from 0 to 14: 7 is neutral (pure water), below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic.
Typical pH values: lime juice about 2, coffee about 5, pure water 7, household ammonia about 12.
pH is defined from the hydrogen ion (hydronium) concentration as its negative logarithm, so the more hydrogen ions a solution holds, the lower its pH.

title: Each pH step is ten times
description: The pH scale is logarithmic: each whole step is a tenfold change in acidity, so lime juice (pH 2) is about a thousand times as acidic as coffee (pH 5).

facts.text: Each whole number on the pH scale is a tenfold change: water at pH 5 is ten times more acidic than water at pH 6.
Lime juice at about pH 2 is three steps below coffee at about pH 5, so it is about 10 x 10 x 10 = 1,000 times more acidic.

title: Neutralization
description: An acid and a base cancel each other out: hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions join into water, and the leftover ions form a salt. New substances form, so it is a chemical change.

facts.text: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide neutralize each other to form sodium chloride (table salt) and water.
In neutralization, hydrogen (hydronium) ions from the acid combine with hydroxide ions from the base to form water, and the reaction also yields a salt.
To a chemist a salt is any ionic compound made of a positive ion other than H+ and a negative ion other than OH-; a typical acid-base neutralization makes a salt and water.
A strong acid and a strong base in matching amounts give a neutral solution, pH 7; other pairings can leave the salt solution slightly acidic or slightly basic.
Neutralization makes new substances (a salt and water) from an acid and a base, so it is a chemical change.

title: Antacids neutralize stomach acid
description: Antacids are bases: milk of magnesia (magnesium hydroxide) and calcium carbonate neutralize some of the stomach's hydrochloric acid.

facts.text: Antacids are bases: milk of magnesia (magnesium hydroxide) releases hydroxide ions that neutralize stomach acid, and calcium carbonate antacids neutralize it while giving off carbon dioxide.

title: Acid-base indicators
description: An indicator changes color with pH. Red cabbage anthocyanins run from red (acid) through purple (neutral) to greenish-yellow (base); litmus, from lichens, turns red in acid and blue in base.

facts.text: An indicator is a substance that changes color when it meets an acid or a base; in pigments like red cabbage anthocyanins, pH changes the molecule's structure, which changes its color.
Red cabbage gets its color from pH-sensitive anthocyanins: very acidic solutions turn them red, neutral ones purplish, mildly basic ones blue to blue-green and strongly basic ones greenish-yellow.
Litmus is a mixture of colored compounds from several lichen species that grow in the Netherlands; it turns red in acids and blue in bases and is the oldest, most commonly used acid-base indicator.

title: Hydrangeas and soil pH
description: Hydrangeas bloom blue in acidic soil and pink in alkaline soil, because acidic soil makes aluminum available and aluminum turns the flowers blue.

facts.text: Hydrangeas bloom blue in acidic soil, where aluminum is more available to the roots and reaches the flowers, and pink in alkaline soil, where aluminum is less available.

title: What causes acid rain, and how it was cut
description: Acid rain, first described by Robert Angus Smith in 1852, comes mostly from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning fossil fuels; it harms lakes, forests and stone. US power plant SO2 fell 96 percent from 1990 to 2023.

facts.text: The Scottish chemist Robert Angus Smith discovered acid rain in 1852 while studying rainwater near industrial cities in England and Scotland, and described it in his 1872 book Air and Rain.

Acid rain comes mainly from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides; a little comes from volcanoes, but most from burning fossil fuels in power plants, vehicles and industry, and they react in the air to form sulfuric and nitric acids that fall as rain, snow, fog or dry particles.
Acid rain leaches aluminum from soil into lakes and streams and strips nutrients trees need; at pH 5 most fish eggs cannot hatch; it also wears away detail on stone and metal statues and monuments.
The US Acid Rain Program, created by the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990, was the first national cap-and-trade program, capping power plants' sulfur dioxide and letting them trade allowances.
Between 1990 and 2023, annual sulfur dioxide emissions from US power plants fell by 96 percent (EPA).

title: How acidic acid rain is
description: Normal rain is already slightly acidic (about pH 5.6) from carbonic acid; acid rain usually measures 4.2 to 4.4, more than ten times as acidic.

facts.text: Normal rain has a pH of about 5.6: it is slightly acidic because carbon dioxide dissolves in it and forms weak carbonic acid.
Acid rain usually has a pH between 4.2 and 4.4.
Acid rain at pH 4.2 to 4.4 is 1.2 to 1.4 pH steps below normal rain at 5.6, so it is more than ten times as acidic.

title: Why the ocean is acidifying
description: The ocean absorbs about 30 percent of the CO2 released into the air; dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions.

facts.text: The ocean absorbs about 30 percent of the carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere (NOAA, 2026), and ocean acidification is the long-term drop in ocean pH this causes.
Dissolved carbon dioxide reacts with seawater to form carbonic acid, which breaks apart into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions, making seawater more acidic.

title: How far ocean pH has fallen
description: Since the Industrial Revolution surface-ocean pH has dropped by about 0.1, roughly 30 percent more hydrogen ions, though seawater is still basic. The IPCC (2021) finds such low pH unusual in 2 million years.

facts.text: Since the Industrial Revolution, global average surface-ocean pH has dropped by about 0.1 (0.11), about a 30 percent increase in hydrogen ions, yet surface seawater is still basic (NOAA).

The IPCC (2021) found it virtually certain that human CO2 emissions are the main driver of current surface-ocean acidification, and surface-ocean pH as low as in recent decades unusual in the last 2 million years.

title: Acidification and shell builders
description: Extra hydrogen ions use up carbonate ions, the building blocks of shells and coral skeletons, so oysters, clams, urchins and corals struggle; Northwest oyster hatcheries fought back by adding a base.

facts.text: Extra hydrogen ions react with carbonate ions, the building blocks of shells and coral skeletons, making them scarcer, so oysters, clams, sea urchins and corals find it harder to build and keep calcium carbonate structures.
Oyster seed production in the US Pacific Northwest plummeted by as much as 80 percent between 2005 and 2009; hatcheries now monitor seawater and add sodium carbonate, a base, to help balance its pH.

title: A battery is a reaction split in two
description: A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy: electrons leave the anode, travel through the outside circuit and are taken up at the cathode. Recharging runs the reaction backward.

facts.text: A battery converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy: at the anode a substance gives up electrons, at the cathode a substance accepts them, and the electrons travel between them through the outside circuit.
A rechargeable battery is restored by driving current through it in reverse, which runs its chemical reaction backward.

title: Acids and bases inside batteries
description: A car's lead-acid battery uses sulfuric acid and an alkaline battery uses potassium hydroxide as the electrolyte, which carries ions inside the battery; in a lemon battery the lemon's acid plays that role.

facts.text: A car's lead-acid battery uses sulfuric acid as its electrolyte, while alkaline batteries use potassium hydroxide, a base.
An electrolyte separates a battery's anode and cathode; charged ions move through it inside the battery while electrons move through the outside circuit.

In a lemon battery the lemon's acid reacts with a zinc strip and loosens electrons; copper pulls electrons more strongly, so they flow through the wire toward it. The energy comes from the metals reacting in the acid.

title: Stomach acid and its jobs
description: Parietal cells in the stomach lining make hydrochloric acid, giving stomach contents a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5; the acid kills much of the bacteria in food and unravels proteins.

facts.text: Parietal cells in the stomach lining produce hydrochloric acid, which gives stomach contents a pH of about 1.5 to 3.5.
Stomach acid kills much of the bacteria swallowed with food and helps unfold (denature) proteins so they are easier to digest.

title: How the stomach survives its own acid
description: A thick bicarbonate-rich mucus neutralizes acid at the lining, keeping the cell surface near neutral; tight junctions seal the lining, and it is replaced every 3 to 6 days. Heartburn is acid in the esophagus.

facts.text: The stomach wall is covered by a thick coat of bicarbonate-rich mucus; the mucus is a physical barrier and its bicarbonate ions neutralize acid.
Across the mucus layer the pH climbs, so the cells of the stomach lining sit near neutral even when the stomach contents are as acidic as pH 2 to 3.
Stomach lining cells meet at tight junctions that block gastric juice from seeping into deeper tissue, and the surface lining is completely replaced every 3 to 6 days.
Heartburn is a painful burning feeling in the chest or throat that happens when stomach acid backs up into the esophagus, the tube from the mouth to the stomach.

title: Water is both acid and base
description: Water is amphiprotic: it can donate or accept a hydrogen ion. A tiny fraction of water molecules trade, making equal numbers of hydronium and hydroxide ions, which is why pure water is neutral, pH 7 at 25 C.

facts.text: Water is amphiprotic, able to donate or accept a hydrogen ion; to a very slight extent water molecules trade them (autoionization), making equal numbers of hydronium and hydroxide ions.
At 25 °C pure water holds 1.0 x 10^-7 moles per liter each of hydronium and hydroxide ions (one ten-millionth), which gives pH 7, neutral; more hydronium lowers the pH, more hydroxide raises it.

title: The big four elements of life
description: Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen make up about 96 percent of the human body's mass and are common to all living things.

facts.text: Four elements, oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen, make up about 96 percent of the human body's mass, and all four are common to all living organisms.
By mass, the human body is about 65 percent oxygen, 18 percent carbon, 10 percent hydrogen and 3 percent nitrogen.

title: Oxygen by mass, hydrogen by headcount
description: Oxygen is the body's top element by mass because it sits in the body's water and its atoms are heavy; counted atom by atom, light hydrogen is the most common.

facts.text: Up to 60 percent of the adult human body is water.
A water molecule is two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom; much of the body's oxygen and hydrogen is in its water, and an oxygen atom is far heavier than a hydrogen atom.
By number of atoms, hydrogen is the most common element in the human body: more than 60 percent of the body's atoms are hydrogen.

title: Carbohydrates and glucose
description: Carbohydrates are built from carbon, hydrogen and oxygen with the general formula (CH2O)n; glucose, C6H12O6, is an important fuel for the body.

facts.text: Carbohydrates have the general formula (CH2O)n; the name means carbon (carbo) plus the components of water (hydrate).
Glucose, C6H12O6, is an important energy source in humans; cells release its energy in cellular respiration.

title: Starch, glycogen and cellulose
description: Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all chains of glucose. Plants store starch and animals store glycogen, but human enzymes cannot break the links in cellulose.

facts.text: Starch is a chain of glucose units; plants store extra glucose as starch in parts such as potato tubers and the seeds of corn, wheat and rice.
Humans and other vertebrates store glucose as glycogen, mostly in liver and muscle cells.
Cellulose is also a chain of glucose units; it makes up about 90 percent of cotton and about 50 percent of wood.
Starch and cellulose link their glucose units differently; human digestive enzymes cannot break cellulose's links, while cows digest it with the help of microbes in their gut.

title: Proteins are chains of amino acids
description: A protein is a chain of hundreds or thousands of amino acids drawn from 20 types, in an order set by a gene.

facts.text: Proteins are chains of hundreds or thousands of amino acids, drawn from 20 different types.
A protein's gene sets its unique order of amino acids, and that sequence determines the protein's 3D shape and its job.
Every amino acid contains nitrogen, in its amino group.

title: A protein's shape is its job
description: Proteins fold into shapes that set their jobs, from keratin in hair to enzymes; heat and chemicals can unfold them for good (denaturation).

facts.text: Proteins do many jobs: some are structural, like keratin in hair and nails, some carry substances around the body, and many are enzymes.
Heat, pH changes and some chemicals can permanently change a protein's shape and function (denaturation); frying an egg denatures the albumin in the egg white, which turns from clear to white.

title: What a fat is
description: A fat is glycerol with three fatty acids. Fats do not dissolve in water; straight saturated chains pack into solids, kinked unsaturated chains stay liquid.

facts.text: A fat molecule, or triglyceride, is a glycerol with three fatty acids attached.
Fats and other lipids are nonpolar and hydrophobic (water-fearing), so they do not dissolve in water.

Saturated fatty acids have only single bonds and are straight, so they pack tightly and are solid at room temperature, like butter; double bonds put kinks in unsaturated fatty acids, keeping oils such as olive oil liquid.

title: Why the body needs fat
description: Fat stores the most energy per gram, insulates, builds cell membranes and carries the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

facts.text: A gram of fat provides 9 calories, compared with 4 for a gram of carbohydrate or protein.
Cells store energy for the long term as fat; lipids also insulate animals and are an important part of all cell membranes.
Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble: the body absorbs them more easily in the presence of dietary fat.

title: Plants are built from air
description: Van Helmont's willow gained 164 pounds while its soil lost about 2 ounces; he credited water, but most of a plant's building material is carbon taken from carbon dioxide in the air.

facts.text: In the 1600s, Jan Baptista van Helmont grew a 5-pound willow in 200 pounds of soil for five years; it reached 169 pounds while the soil lost only about 2 ounces.
Van Helmont concluded that the tree's extra 164 pounds came from water alone; he did not account for the air.
Plants take the carbon that makes up most of their building material from carbon dioxide in the air, not from the soil.

title: The photosynthesis equation
description: Using light captured by chlorophyll, plants turn six carbon dioxide and six water molecules into one glucose and six oxygen molecules; the oxygen comes from the water.

facts.text: In photosynthesis, six carbon dioxide molecules and six water molecules, using light energy captured by chlorophyll, make one glucose molecule and six oxygen molecules.
The oxygen that plants give off comes from splitting water, not from carbon dioxide, as experiments with oxygen-18-labeled water showed in 1941.

title: Cellular respiration
description: Cells combine glucose with oxygen, mostly in mitochondria, releasing energy and giving off carbon dioxide and water; the carbon you breathe out came from your food.

facts.text: Cellular respiration combines glucose with oxygen, releasing energy and producing carbon dioxide and water: C6H12O6 + 6O2 gives 6CO2 + 6H2O.
In both plant and animal cells, mitochondria carry out cellular respiration, using oxygen and giving off carbon dioxide as waste.
The carbon in the carbon dioxide you breathe out comes from the food molecules your cells broke down; the lungs move that carbon dioxide out of the blood.
The products of photosynthesis (glucose and oxygen) are the reactants of cellular respiration, and the products of respiration (carbon dioxide and water) are the reactants of photosynthesis.

title: Energy in small change: ATP
description: Cells release food's energy in small steps instead of one burst, capturing it in ATP, the cell's energy currency.

facts.text: Cells capture the energy released from food in ATP, often called the energy currency of the cell.
Cells release food's energy in small steps rather than in a single destructive burst, which lets them capture it.

title: Enzymes, the catalysts of life
description: Enzymes are catalysts, nearly all proteins, that speed up reactions by lowering the energy needed to start them and are left unchanged; salivary amylase breaks starch into sugars.

facts.text: Starchy foods such as rice and potatoes taste slightly sweet when chewed because the enzyme amylase in saliva breaks tasteless starch into sugars, including glucose.
Enzymes are catalysts for the reactions of life: they speed reactions up by lowering the activation energy, the energy needed to get started, and almost all are proteins.
An enzyme is left unchanged by the reaction it speeds up, so after releasing its products it can work again.

title: Active sites: a fit, not a force
description: A substrate binds in the enzyme's active site, so each enzyme is specific; the picture moved from Fischer's lock and key (1894) to Koshland's induced fit (1958). Heat and extreme pH can denature enzymes.

facts.text: The molecule an enzyme acts on, its substrate, binds at the enzyme's active site; the close fit makes each enzyme specific to its substrates.
In 1894 Emil Fischer compared an enzyme and its substrate to a lock and key; in 1958 Daniel Koshland proposed induced fit, in which the active site reshapes as the substrate binds.
High temperatures and extreme pH can denature enzymes, changing their shape so they stop working.

title: From willow bark to aspirin
description: Willow bark was an ancient remedy; chemists isolated salicin, modified salicylic acid into gentler acetylsalicylic acid in 1897, and learned in 1971 that it blocks prostaglandin production.

facts.text: Chinese and Greek civilizations used willow bark as medicine more than 2,000 years ago; in 1828 Johann Büchner isolated a substance from willow that he named salicin.
Salicylic acid, made from salicin, eased pain but often irritated the stomach.
At Bayer, Arthur Eichengrün set chemist Felix Hoffmann the task of making a better salicylic acid; in 1897 Hoffmann made acetylsalicylic acid, which irritated the stomach less.

Aspirin was sold for decades before anyone knew how it worked; in 1971 John Vane showed it blocks the body's making of prostaglandins, which are involved in pain, fever and inflammation, and he shared the 1982 Nobel Prize.

title: Designing and testing medicines
description: Chemists can design a drug to fit a target enzyme's shape, as with HIV protease inhibitors (first used in 1995); new drugs are then tested in people in phases, starting with safety and dosage.

facts.text: Knowing the crystal structure of the HIV protease enzyme was critical for designing drugs that block it; the first entered clinical use in 1995, a great success of structure-based drug design.

A new drug is tested in people in phases: Phase 1 (20 to 100 volunteers) studies safety and dosage; Phase 2 (up to several hundred people) and Phase 3 (300 to 3,000) test whether it works and watch for side effects.

title: The dose makes the poison
description: Paracelsus taught that whether a substance harms depends on the dose; by that principle even water is poisonous in a large enough amount.

facts.text: Paracelsus (1493 to 1541), a German-Swiss physician, wrote: "All things are poison and nothing is without poison. Solely the dose determines that a thing is not a poison."
Paracelsus introduced the concept of dose and studied poisons by experiment; the amount a person is exposed to is central to toxicology, the science of poisons.
By the dose concept, even a substance as harmless as water is poisonous if too much of it is taken in.

title: Poison or medicine: the foxglove
description: Foxglove is toxic, yet in 1785 William Withering showed that small, carefully adjusted doses treated the swelling of heart failure; digitalis drugs are still prescribed.

facts.text: In 1785 William Withering published a study of foxglove showing that small, nontoxic doses of its leaf treated dropsy, the swelling that came with heart failure; he also described the signs of digitalis poisoning.
Drugs containing digitalis, foxglove's active compound, are still prescribed today.

title: Plants respire too
description: Plant cells have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts: plants make sugar by photosynthesis and burn some of it in cellular respiration for ATP.

facts.text: Plant cells have mitochondria as well as chloroplasts; plants use the sugars they make in cellular respiration, generating ATP in their mitochondria.

title: The Maillard reaction
description: When food is heated, its sugars react with the amino acids of proteins, browning it and creating new flavors and aromas. A wet surface stays near water's boiling point, so browning waits until it dries.

facts.text: The Maillard reaction is a chemical reaction between sugars and the amino acids of proteins in heated food; it browns food and creates new flavors and aromas, as in bread crust, fried foods, seared meat and coffee.
The Maillard reaction is named after the French scientist Louis-Camille Maillard, who first described it.
While food is very wet, its surface cannot get hotter than the boiling point of water, so the Maillard reaction takes off only once the surface dries out.

title: Caramelization
description: Heat alone breaks sugar down into new brown, flavorful compounds; unlike the Maillard reaction, no protein is involved.

facts.text: Caramelization is the action of heat on sugar alone: at high temperatures sugar breaks down into new compounds with a brown color and new flavors, with no protein involved.

title: Yeast makes bread rise
description: Yeast ferments sugars in dough into carbon dioxide and alcohol; gluten traps the gas, the oven expands it, kills the yeast and drives off most of the alcohol.

facts.text: Yeast in bread dough feeds on sugars and turns them into carbon dioxide gas and alcohol (ethanol), a process called fermentation; the gas makes the dough rise.
Gluten, a stretchy protein network in wheat dough, traps the carbon dioxide bubbles, so the dough expands; the trapped gas leaves bread's airy holes.
In the oven, the trapped gas expands and the dough rises further, the heat kills the yeast, and most of the alcohol evaporates.

title: Baking soda and baking powder
description: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when moistened and heated, much more with an acidic ingredient; baking powder packs its own acid with the soda.

facts.text: Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) releases carbon dioxide when it is moistened and heated, and releases much more gas when an acidic ingredient such as honey, molasses or cocoa is present.
Baking powder contains sodium bicarbonate together with one or more acids, which react to produce carbon dioxide when the batter is moistened and heated.

title: The two-ended soap molecule
description: Water alone can't lift grease. A soap molecule has a water-attracting head and an oil-attracting tail, so it can hold both; soap itself is made from fats or oils and an alkali.

facts.text: Water alone cannot remove grease or oil, because oil and water do not mix.
A soap molecule has a head that is attracted to water and a long tail that is attracted to oil and grease, so one molecule can hold on to both.
Soap is made by reacting fats or oils, such as tallow or vegetable oil, with a strong alkali, a reaction called saponification.

title: Micelles carry grease away
description: Soap tails dive into grease while heads face the water; soap molecules surround the grease in clusters called micelles, which stay suspended and rinse away.

facts.text: In soapy water, soap molecules surround grease and dirt with their tails inside and heads facing the water, forming clusters called micelles that stay suspended and are rinsed away.

title: Why bleach must never be mixed
description: Household bleach (sodium hypochlorite) mixed with ammonia makes toxic chloramine gases; mixed with acids, it releases chlorine gas. Both harm the eyes, nose, throat and lungs.

facts.text: Household bleach is a solution of sodium hypochlorite in water.
Mixing bleach with ammonia, which is found in some glass cleaners, produces toxic gases called chloramines.
Mixing bleach with acidic products, such as vinegar, some toilet bowl cleaners and rust removers, releases chlorine gas.
These gases irritate the eyes, nose and throat and cause coughing and breathing problems; higher exposures can damage the lungs.
Urine contains ammonia, so health officials warn to take care using bleach when cleaning litter boxes, diaper pails and toilets.

title: Safe habits with cleaners
description: Health agencies advise never mixing bleach with other cleaners, ventilating and following labels; after breathing fumes, get to fresh air and call a poison center.

facts.text: The CDC advises never mixing household bleach with any other cleaner or disinfectant, using it with good ventilation and following the label directions.
Poison Control advises anyone exposed to fumes from mixed cleaners to leave the area immediately for fresh air and call a poison center (1-800-222-1222 in the US).

title: How dyes make color
description: A dye colors a material by absorbing some colors of light and reflecting the rest; the reflected light is the color you see.

facts.text: An object's color depends on which colors of light it absorbs and which it reflects: a red object reflects red light and absorbs the rest, and a black object absorbs all colors.
A dye is a substance used to give color to textiles and other materials so that the color is not readily altered by washing, heat or light.

title: Mordants fix dyes
description: Some dyes need a mordant, a metal salt that soaks into the fiber and reacts with the dye to form a less soluble form held to the cloth. The name comes from Latin mordere, to bite.

facts.text: A mordant is a metal salt taken up by the fiber that reacts with the dye to form a less soluble form held to the fabric; the word comes from the Latin mordere, to bite.

title: Perkin's mauve, the first synthetic dye
description: In 1856 the 18-year-old William Henry Perkin, trying to make quinine from coal-tar chemicals, made mauve instead: the first commercialized synthetic dye. Before that, dyes came from plants and animals.

facts.text: In 1856, 18-year-old William Henry Perkin, trying to make the antimalarial drug quinine from coal-tar chemicals, made mauve instead, the first commercialized synthetic dye.
Perkin patented his dye in 1856.
Before synthetic dyes, dyes came from plants and animals: blue indigo from plant leaves, red from the roots of the madder plant, and Tyrian purple from the glands of a sea snail.

title: Smells are airborne molecules
description: Smelling is detecting chemicals in the air, so only substances that release molecules into the air (volatile ones) have a smell. Warmth helps more molecules escape.

facts.text: Smell is the detection of chemicals carried in the air.
Odor molecules are volatile: they vaporize readily into the air.
As a liquid warms, more of its molecules have enough energy to escape into the air, so its vapor pressure rises.

title: Diffusion carries smells
description: Molecules spread from where they are concentrated to where they are sparse (diffusion). Gas molecules are fast but collide constantly, so a smell's journey is a slow zigzag.

facts.text: Diffusion is molecules spreading out from where they are concentrated to where they are not, which is how the aroma of a hot pizza spreads through a room.
Gas molecules move at hundreds of meters per second, but they keep colliding with other molecules and changing direction, so their overall spread is much slower.

title: Plastics that remelt and plastics that don't
description: Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be remelted and reshaped, so they recycle readily. Thermosets cross-link as they harden and cannot be remelted.

facts.text: Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be remelted and reshaped, which makes them readily recyclable.
Thermosetting plastics, such as epoxy and polyurethane, cross-link as they harden and cannot be remelted; old thermosets are usually ground up for use as fillers.

title: How plastic is recycled
description: Recycling sorts plastics by type, grinds them into flakes, washes them, separates them by density in water and melts them into pellets. Heat and grinding shorten polymer chains, so quality drops.

facts.text: In mechanical recycling, plastic is sorted by type, ground into small flakes, washed with hot water and detergent, then melted and formed into pellets used to make new products.
In a water tank, plastic flakes separate by density: PET bottle flakes sink, while flakes from caps made of polypropylene or HDPE float.
The heat and grinding of recycling break some of plastic's long polymer chains, so recycled plastic usually doesn't match new plastic and often goes into less-demanding products.

title: Making glass from sand
description: Glass is mostly sand (silica), which melts only above 1,700 °C. Soda lowers the melting point but makes glass that dissolves in water; lime makes it insoluble again: soda-lime glass.

facts.text: Everyday glass is made from three main materials: sand (silicon dioxide, or silica), limestone and sodium carbonate (soda).
Sand (crystalline silica) melts only above 1,700 °C; adding soda (sodium oxide) as a flux lowers the melting temperature dramatically.
Glass of silica and soda alone dissolves in water; adding lime (calcium oxide, from limestone) makes it insoluble again, giving soda-lime glass.

title: Glass is an amorphous solid
description: Molten glass is cooled too fast for crystals to form, so its particles freeze in a disordered jumble: an amorphous solid. Old panes thicker at the bottom are not proof that glass flows.

facts.text: Glass is made by cooling the molten ingredients quickly enough to prevent crystals from forming, so it is an amorphous solid, without the long-range order of a crystal.
Old window panes are sometimes thicker at the bottom because of how they were made, not because glass flows; room-temperature glass would take longer than the age of the universe to sag noticeably.

title: Fuels store chemical energy
description: Fuels store chemical energy in the bonds of their molecules; burning converts it to heat. Natural gas is odorless, so a smelly chemical is added to reveal leaks.

facts.text: Chemical energy is energy stored in the bonds of atoms and molecules; petroleum and natural gas store it, and burning converts it to heat, as when gasoline burns in a car engine.
Natural gas is colorless and odorless, so gas companies add mercaptan, a chemical with a strong unpleasant smell, to help people detect leaks.
Oil and natural gas formed over millions of years from the remains of plants and animals, changed by heat and pressure after being buried.

title: Hydrocarbon fuels
description: Gasoline and natural gas are hydrocarbons, compounds of only carbon and hydrogen. Natural gas is mostly methane (CH4). Gasoline is made from crude oil, first separated by distillation.

facts.text: Hydrocarbons are compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen; they are the main ingredients of petroleum and natural gas, and burning them releases heat and forms carbon dioxide and water.
Natural gas is mostly methane (CH4), the simplest hydrocarbon, made of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms.

Gasoline is made from crude oil at refineries; heated crude oil is first separated by distillation into fractions by boiling point, and the lightest fractions, including gasoline, rise to the top of the tower.

title: Hard water and soap scum
description: Calcium and magnesium in hard water react with soap to form insoluble scum, wasting soap. Detergents work like soap but are made from petroleum and don't form scum, so they work in hard water.

facts.text: Hard water contains calcium and magnesium, which react with soap to form an insoluble scum (soap scum) that reduces soap's cleaning power.
Detergents work like soap, with a charged head and a long oil-attracting tail, but are made from petroleum products rather than natural fats, and they don't form scum in hard water.

title: What alchemists were trying to do
description: Alchemists tried to turn base metals such as lead or copper into gold or silver, hoped to make a philosophers' stone that would do it, and sought cures and longer life.

facts.text: Isaac Newton wrote and transcribed about a million words on alchemy, over some thirty years, and kept the work largely hidden from his colleagues.
Alchemists tried to transform base metals such as lead or copper into silver or gold, and to find a cure for disease and a way of extending life.
Alchemists hoped to prepare the philosophers' stone, a material supposedly able to transmute base metals into gold.

title: What alchemy left to chemistry
description: Alchemists never made gold, but they built and described laboratory apparatus and techniques (distillation, sublimation, filtration, the alembic, the hot-water bath) and left chemistry its name and several words.

facts.text: Alchemists described apparatus for distillation, sublimation and filtration in detail.
The alembic, a distillation apparatus used chiefly by alchemists, had a vessel for the material being distilled, a head to receive and condense the vapor, and a receiver for the distilled liquid.
The word alchemy comes from the Arabic al-kimiya, and the word chemistry grew out of alchemy.
The words alcohol, elixir and alembic come from Arabic alchemy.
The ancient alchemist Maria is credited with gentle, even heating in a bath of hot water instead of an open flame; her name survives in the cook's bain-marie.

title: Boyle's law
description: At constant temperature, the volume of a trapped gas is inversely proportional to its pressure: double the pressure and the volume halves. Boyle published it in 1662 after air-pump experiments with Robert Hooke.

facts.text: In 1659 Robert Boyle and Robert Hooke completed an air pump and used it to study the properties of air.
Boyle's law, published by Robert Boyle in 1662: at constant temperature, a gas's volume is inversely proportional to its pressure, so doubling the pressure halves the volume.
Pushing in the plunger of an airtight syringe compresses the gas inside into a smaller volume, and its pressure increases.
When you inhale, your chest cavity expands and your lung volume grows; the larger volume means lower pressure (Boyle's law), so air flows into the lungs.
The volumes of liquids and solids are very nearly independent of pressure, while a gas takes the shape and volume of its container.

title: Boyle and experimental chemistry
description: In The Sceptical Chymist (1661) Boyle attacked older Aristotelian ideas about what matter is made of; his reliance on experiment earned him the name 'father of chemistry', though he also pursued alchemy all his life.

facts.text: Boyle's 1661 book The Sceptical Chymist attacked the Aristotelian and other accepted ideas of the time about the composition of matter.
Boyle's work relied on experiment and observation, and he argued so strongly for applying chemistry to the study of nature and medicine that he was later called the 'father of chemistry'.
Boyle pursued transmutational alchemy all his life, trying to discover how to turn base metals into gold.

title: Lavoisier overturns phlogiston
description: Phlogiston theory said burnable things lost phlogiston when they burned. Lavoisier showed that burned metals gain mass because oxygen from the air combines with them.

facts.text: Phlogiston theory held that burnable things such as charcoal and metals contained phlogiston, which they released into the air as they burned.
Metals such as lead and tin weigh more after they are burned; Lavoisier showed this is because oxygen from the air combines with the metal.
Antoine Lavoisier is known as the father of modern chemistry, for his emphasis on careful experimentation.

title: Lavoisier's names and list of elements
description: In 1787 Lavoisier and colleagues published a naming method still at the base of chemical names; oxygen and hydrogen replaced old names; his 1789 textbook listed 33 elements, including light and caloric.

facts.text: In 1787 Lavoisier and three colleagues (Guyton de Morveau, Berthollet and Fourcroy) published a new method of naming chemical substances, still the basis of chemical names today.
Lavoisier's new names replaced 'dephlogisticated air' with oxygen ('acid former') and 'inflammable air' with hydrogen ('water former').
Lavoisier showed that water is not a simple substance but is made of hydrogen and oxygen.
Lavoisier's 1789 textbook, the Elementary Treatise of Chemistry, listed 33 substances he considered elements, beginning with light and caloric (heat).
Light and caloric, on Lavoisier's list of elements, are not chemical elements.

Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier worked with her husband as a scientific collaborator: she made drawings for his works, including the laboratory illustrations in his textbook, and translated English works for him.
Lavoisier held a share in the General Farm, a company that collected taxes; during the Reign of Terror he was guillotined, on May 8, 1794.

title: Dalton's atomic theory
description: Dalton proposed that all matter is made of atoms, that each element has its own kind of atom with a characteristic mass, that compounds join atoms in small whole-number ratios, and that chemical changes rearrange atoms without creating or destroying them.

facts.text: Dalton set out his atomic theory in A New System of Chemical Philosophy, published in parts from 1808.

Dalton's theory: matter is made of tiny atoms; an element has one type of atom with a characteristic mass; compounds join atoms of different elements in small whole-number ratios; chemical changes rearrange atoms, never creating or destroying them.
Dalton proposed that water is HO, one atom of hydrogen with one of oxygen; water is actually hydrogen and oxygen in a 2 to 1 ratio, H2O.

title: Dalton's road from weather to atoms
description: Dalton kept daily weather records for 57 years; studying the gases of the air, and how each gas in a mixture acts independently, led him to atomism.

facts.text: John Dalton kept daily weather records from 1787 until his death in 1844, about 57 years.
Dalton reached atomism by way of meteorology: studying the air, he concluded that each gas in a mixture exerts its pressure independently of the others.

title: Marie Curie's new elements
description: Curie named radioactivity, found pitchblende more radioactive than uranium, and with Pierre Curie announced polonium and radium in 1898; she won Nobel Prizes in physics (1903) and chemistry (1911).

facts.text: Marie Curie named radioactivity, the rays given off by uranium that Henri Becquerel discovered; the Curies first used the term in their 1898 work.
Curie found that pitchblende, a uranium ore, was much more radioactive than pure uranium itself.
In 1898 Marie and Pierre Curie announced two new elements: polonium, named after Marie's native Poland, and radium.
In 1903 Marie Curie shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, becoming the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.
In 1911 Marie Curie alone won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, for discovering radium and polonium; she remains the only woman to win in two different fields.
Marie Curie died in 1934 of aplastic anemia caused by radiation exposure.

title: Isolating radium
description: To prove radium was a real element Curie needed it in a demonstrable amount; tracking radioactivity through her separations, she got a tenth of a gram of almost pure radium chloride from several tons of ore.

facts.text: To show that radium was a new element, the Curies had to produce it in a demonstrable amount, which needed tons of costly pitchblende.
Curie tracked the new elements by their radioactivity: each time she removed some of a known element, such as bismuth, the residue left behind was more active.
After thousands of crystallizations, Marie Curie isolated one decigram (a tenth of a gram) of almost pure radium chloride from several tons of starting material.

title: X-ray diffraction
description: Rosalind Franklin used X-ray diffraction at King's College London: X-rays scatter off the atoms of a crystal at angles that reveal how the atoms are arranged.

facts.text: From 1951, at King's College London, the chemist Rosalind Franklin applied X-ray diffraction methods to the study of DNA.
In X-ray diffraction, X-rays scatter off a crystal at angles that indicate how its atoms are arranged.

title: Photo 51
description: In May 1952 Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling made Photo 51, a 62-hour exposure whose X-shaped pattern showed DNA's strands are helical.

facts.text: In May 1952 Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling exposed a DNA fiber to X-rays for a total of 62 hours to make Photograph 51.
Photo 51 showed an X-shaped pattern, which indicated to Franklin that DNA's strands are helical; it became some of the clearest evidence for DNA's double helix.

title: Credit for DNA's structure
description: Wilkins showed Photo 51 to Watson without Franklin's knowledge; her own paper ran in the same 1953 issue of Nature as Watson and Crick's; she died in 1958, before the 1962 Nobel, which is not awarded after death.

facts.text: In early 1953 Franklin's colleague Maurice Wilkins showed Photo 51 to James Watson without her knowledge or agreement.
In April 1953 Watson and Crick published their DNA model in Nature, and Franklin and Gosling's own paper on DNA's structure appeared in the same issue.
Rosalind Franklin died of ovarian cancer in 1958, aged 37.
In 1962 Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize for DNA's structure; Franklin could not be included because the Nobel is not awarded after death.

title: Nylon
description: Wallace Carothers's DuPont team invented nylon in 1935 as a synthetic silk made from widely available compounds; nylon stockings launched in 1939, and in the war nylon went into parachutes.

facts.text: Nylon was invented in 1935 by Wallace Carothers's research team at DuPont, as a synthetic silk.
Nylon was a useful fiber made by chemical synthesis from compounds readily available from air, water, and coal or petroleum.
Nylon went into production in 1939, and nylon stockings were a sensation at that year's New York World's Fair; in World War II nylon was used for parachutes.

title: Teflon, found by accident
description: In 1938 Roy Plunkett found that tetrafluoroethylene gas in a cylinder had turned into a white solid: no gas came out, but the cylinder weighed the same. The solid, Teflon, is heat resistant, inert and slippery.

facts.text: Teflon was discovered by accident in 1938 by Roy Plunkett at DuPont.
Plunkett had stored tetrafluoroethylene gas in small cylinders; when he opened one, no gas came out, yet the cylinder weighed the same as before, and inside was a white powder.
The tetrafluoroethylene gas in Plunkett's cylinder had turned into a new solid substance, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), sold as Teflon.
Plunkett found the white powder was heat resistant, chemically inert and so low in friction that most other substances would not stick to it.
Teflon's first uses were industrial; Teflon pots and pans came years after its discovery.

title: Green chemistry: prevent, don't clean up
description: Green chemistry designs chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances, preventing pollution at its source rather than cleaning it up afterward.

facts.text: Green chemistry is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use or generation of hazardous substances.

Green chemistry reduces pollution at its source; that is not the same as cleaning up pollution (remediation), which treats waste after it is made, for example by separating hazardous chemicals from other materials.
In 1998 Paul Anastas and John Warner set out the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry; the first says it is better to prevent waste than to treat or clean it up afterward.

title: Atom economy
description: Atom economy asks that a reaction's final product contain as much of the starting materials as possible; BHC's ibuprofen route cut six steps to three and raised atom use from under 40 to about 80 percent.

facts.text: Atom economy, the second principle of green chemistry: design syntheses so the final product contains the maximum proportion of the starting materials, wasting few or no atoms.
An older way of making the painkiller ibuprofen took six steps with under 40 percent of the atoms used ending up in product; BHC Company's route takes three steps with about 80 percent.
BHC Company's ibuprofen process, which recovers and reuses its waste byproduct, won a US Presidential Green Chemistry Challenge Award in 1997.

title: The 'chemical-free' myth
description: Everything we eat, drink and live in is made of chemicals, natural and synthetic, so no product is chemical-free; the RSC's 2008 million-pound offer and a blank 2014 'overview' made the point.

facts.text: In 2008 the Royal Society of Chemistry offered a million pounds to the first member of the public who could hand over any material it considered 100% chemical free.
Everything we eat, drink, drive, play with and live in is made of chemicals, and both natural and synthetic chemicals are essential for life.
The RSC said the word 'chemical' had been misused in advertising and marketing as if it meant poison, and set out to reclaim it.

In 2014 two chemists sent Nature Chemistry 'A comprehensive overview of chemical-free consumer products', which examined lotions, supplements, cleaners, foods and drinks; its list of truly chemical-free products was empty, and the journal shared it on its blog.

title: Natural and synthetic molecules
description: A molecule is the same whether it comes from a plant or a factory: natural and synthetic vitamin C are chemically identical.

facts.text: Natural and synthetic vitamin C (L-ascorbic acid) are chemically identical, with no known differences in how they act in the body.
